ATT&CKT1486
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem DeviceFileEvents
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
| where ActionType in ("FileRenamed","FileModified")
| summarize files = dcount(FileName) by DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, bin(Timestamp, 1m)
| where files > 200    // empirical: > 200 unique-file renames in 1m by one account on one host
                       //            is well above the P99 of legitimate bulk-tooling
| order by files desc

ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)
| where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
| where EventType in ("FileRenamed","FileModified")
| summarize files = dcount(TargetFileName)

| where files > 200    // P99 of legit bulk-tooling per-minute rename volume
| order by files desc

LSASS process access / dump (credential theft) Actions on Objectives High

ATT&CKT1003.001 T1003
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes DeviceEvents
DeviceEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| where ActionType == "OpenProcessApiCall"
| where FileName =~ "lsass.exe"
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("MsSense.exe","MsMpEng.exe","csrss.exe",
                                          "svchost.exe","wininit.exe","services.exe",
                                          "lsm.exe","SearchProtocolHost.exe")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessFolderPath, AccountName
| order by Timestamp desc
// SecurityEvent EventID 4663 = object access. AccessMask 0x10 / 0x40 / 0x1010
// indicate read access to lsass.exe — credential-dump signature. Audit
// Object Access > Audit File System policy required.
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventID == 4663
| where ObjectName endswith "\lsass.exe"
| where Account !endswith "$"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, ObjectName, ProcessName,
          AccessMask, AccessReason
| order by TimeGenerated desc

GhostAction CI/CD secret exfiltration egress to attacker infrastructure AIActions on Objectives Medium
Hunts outbound connections from any host (self-hosted GitHub Actions runners, developer workstations, CI agents) to the GhostAction campaign's exfiltration IPs and hostnames used to POST harvested PyPI/npm/DockerHub/GitHub/AWS secrets. Article-specific because it pins the exact attacker infrastructure GitGuardian and StepSecurity tied to the 3,325-secret GitHub-workflow theft. Rationale: Uses the exact GhostAction exfil IPs (45.139.104.115, 216.126.225.129) and hostnames (bold-dhawan/objective-hopper.45-139-104-115.plesk.page, carte-avantage.com) that GitGuardian and StepSecurity attributed to the campaign; a single connection to any of these from CI/dev infrastructure is a confirmed credential-exfil signal. Cross-checked against: • https://blog.gitguardian.com/ghostaction-campaign-3-325-secrets-stolen/ • https://www.bleepingcomputer.com/news/security/hackers-steal-3-325-secrets-in-ghostaction-github-supply-chain-attack/ • https://www.stepsecurity.io/blog/ghostaction-campaign-over-3-000-secrets-stolen-through-malicious-github-workflows
ATT&CKT1567 T1195.001
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • A threat-intel/EDR sandbox intentionally detonating the GhostAction IOC set for validation
  • An internal purple-team or IR replay reaching the now-defunct endpoints during a tabletop exercise
  • A passive-DNS or attack-surface scanner (e.g. a CTI enrichment service) resolving/probing the hostnames from a known scanner host
  • A DNS sinkhole or proxy that rewrites the destination, causing the flow to appear as a connection to the IOC before being blocked
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("MsSense.exe", "SenseIR.exe", "MsMpEng.exe")
Response runbook
Step 1 (triage): Identify the initiating host and process — is it a self-hosted Actions runner, CI agent, or developer endpoint? Pull InitiatingProcessCommandLine and the surrounding workflow run to confirm a POST of secrets versus a benign scanner. Step 2 (contain): Block 45.139.104.115 / 216.126.225.129 and the three hostnames at egress firewall/proxy, isolate the runner, and immediately rotate every secret exposed to that pipeline (PyPI, npm, DockerHub, GitHub PAT/Actions, AWS keys). Step 3 (hunt): Review the repo's recent workflow-file diffs for an injected 'Github Actions Security' job, enumerate all repos sharing the compromised account/runner, and search 30 days of DNS + proxy logs for any prior resolution of these hostnames.

| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where RemoteIP in ("45.139.104.115","216.126.225.129")

GhostAction exfil-domain DNS resolution (blocked-egress early warning) AICommand & Control High
Hunts DNS queries for the GhostAction exfiltration hostnames from any endpoint or runner, catching a compromised GitHub Action that attempts to resolve the drop point even when egress is blocked (the Harden-Runner block-mode scenario). Distinct from the connection-based UC: DNS fires on attempt, so it surfaces the intent before—or independent of—a successful POST. Rationale: Pivots on the GhostAction exfil hostnames (bold-dhawan/objective-hopper.45-139-104-115.plesk.page, carte-avantage.com) at the DNS layer so a compromised workflow's resolution attempt is caught even under egress-block; a resolution of these dead attacker domains has no legitimate reason to occur. Cross-checked against: • https://blog.gitguardian.com/ghostaction-campaign-3-325-secrets-stolen/ • https://www.stepsecurity.io/blog/ghostaction-campaign-over-3-000-secrets-stolen-through-malicious-github-workflows
ATT&CKT1567 T1071.001
Data sourcesNetwork_Resolution.DNS
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • CTI enrichment / passive-DNS services resolving the hostnames from a designated research host
  • Security-team validation of the IOC feed during detection testing
  • A recursive resolver logging a cached NXDOMAIN lookup triggered by a stale allow/deny-list sync
  • Newsletter/blog-link crawlers or URL-preview bots dereferencing the IOC string embedded in an advisory page
Response runbook
Step 1 (triage): Confirm the querying host and the process context (ContextImageFileName / InitiatingProcessFileName) — a runner, node/python process, or curl resolving these domains is high-confidence malicious; a browser/CTI tool is likely benign. Step 2 (contain): Sinkhole the three hostnames and their IP (45.139.104.115) at internal DNS, freeze the affected repo's Actions runs, and rotate all pipeline secrets. Step 3 (hunt): Correlate with the connection-based UC for any successful egress, diff recent workflow YAML for an injected exfil job, and sweep DNS history org-wide for these names to scope all impacted runners/repos.
DeviceNetworkEvents

| where ActionType == "DnsQueryResponse"
| where RemoteUrl has_any ("bold-dhawan.45-139-104-115.plesk.page","objective-hopper.45-139-104-115.plesk.page","carte-avantage.com")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, RemoteUrl, RemoteIP
| order by Timestamp desc
DnsEvents

| project TimeGenerated, Computer, ClientIP, Name, QueryType, IPAddresses = Result
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Vidar Stealer Unmasked: Code Signing Abuse, Go Loaders and File Inflation

Unit 42 (Palo Alto)
2026-07-07 13 use cases 10 techniques 6 kill-chain phases detected

A cybercrime campaign combined a loader-as-a-service framework and DLL sideloading via a Go-compiled fake MpClient.dll, a novel evasion layer combination. The post Vidar Stealer Unmasked: Code Signing Abuse, Go Loaders and File Inflation appeared first on Unit 42 .

ATT&CKT1021.001 T1027 T1053.005 T1190 T1195.002 T1204.004 T1539 T1547.001 T1555.003 T1574.002

Actions on Objectives
Detected
Reconnaissance. Attacker researches the target — OSINT, scanning, enumeration.
Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad). → [LLM] Oversized (>100 MB) PE dropped in user path - null-byte file inflation (Vidar loader) · Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code. → Fake CAPTCHA / clipboard-injected PowerShell (ClickFix / FakeCaptcha) · PowerShell encoded / obfuscated command · Trusted vendor binary / installer launching unusual children · Article-specific behavioural hunt — Vidar Stealer Unmasked: Code Signing Abuse, Go Loaders and File Inflation
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key. → [LLM] Fake Windows Defender MpClient.dll search-order hijack (Vidar Factory-v3 Cluster B) · Scheduled task created with suspicious image / encoded args
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking. → Beaconing — periodic outbound to small set of destinations · Network connections to article IPs / domains
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage. → [LLM] XMRig Monero mining to pool.supportxmr.com / 136.243.203.109 (Vidar drop) · Infostealer — non-browser process accessing browser cookie/login DBs · Crypto-wallet file/keystore access by non-wallet process
Fake Windows Defender MpClient.dll search-order hijack (Vidar Factory-v3 Cluster B) AIInstallation High
Hunts the Cluster B loader variant that ships a malicious MpClient.dll exporting real Defender API names (MpAllocMemory, MpConfigOpen, etc.) so a legitimate Windows Defender binary side-loads it. Fires when mpclient.dll is loaded/written from any path outside the genuine Windows Defender install directories. Rationale: Uses the article's exact Cluster B artefact (fake MpClient.dll exporting Defender APIs for search-order hijack). Genuine mpclient.dll only ever loads from '\Windows Defender\' paths, so any other location is high-fidelity. Cross-checked against: • https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1574/002/ • https://harfanglab.io/insidethelab/hijackloader-abusing-genuine-certificates/ • https://www.broadcom.com/support/security-center/protection-bulletin/abuse-of-code-signing-certificates-in-lumma-stealer-deployment-via-hijackloader
ATT&CKT1574.002
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Third-party AV/EDR product bundling its own file literally named mpclient.dll (rare)
  • Security-research/malware-analysis VM with copied Defender binaries in a non-standard folder
  • Windows Defender Platform update transiently staging binaries in a temp path before moving to Platform\<version>
  • Backup/imaging software restoring Defender files to an alternate drive letter
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessFolderPath !startswith @"C:\Program Files\Windows Defender" and InitiatingProcessFolderPath !has @"\Windows Defender\Platform\"
Response runbook
1) TRIAGE: Confirm the loading/parent process is NOT a genuine Defender binary (MsMpEng.exe/MpCmdRun.exe) running from Program Files; inspect FolderPath and SHA256 and check the DLL's export table for the mimicked Mp* functions. 2) CONTAIN: Isolate the host, kill the sideloading process tree, and quarantine the rogue mpclient.dll plus its co-located loader EXE. 3) HUNT: Pivot on the loader's write process and hash across the fleet; check for concurrent XMRig egress (supportxmr.com) and Vidar browser-credential/cookie access on the same host.
DeviceImageLoadEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where FileName =~ "mpclient.dll"
| where FolderPath !startswith @"C:\Program Files\Windows Defender"
| where FolderPath !startswith @"C:\Program Files (x86)\Windows Defender"
| where FolderPath !has @"\Windows Defender\Platform\"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessFolderPath, InitiatingProcessCommandLine
| order by Timestamp desc
ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where TargetFileName =~ "mpclient.dll"
| where TargetFilePath !has @"\Windows Defender\"
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, TargetFilePath, TargetFileSHA256,
          ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine, ActorUsername
| order by TimeGenerated desc
title: Rogue Windows Defender MpClient.dll Side-Load
id: 6f1c2e0a-9b4d-4c1e-8a7f-2b9d5e3c1a44
description: Detects mpclient.dll loaded from a directory outside the genuine Windows Defender install path, consistent with the Vidar Factory-v3 Cluster B DLL search-order hijack.
references:
  - https://unit42.paloaltonetworks.com/vidar-stealer-xmrig-miner-campaign-analysis/
author: SOC Detection Engineering
date: 2026/07/08
tags:
  - attack.t1574.002
  - attack.defense_evasion
logsource:
  category: image_load
  product: windows
detection:
  selection:
    ImageLoaded|endswith: '\mpclient.dll'
  filter_defender:
    ImageLoaded|contains: '\Windows Defender\'
  condition: selection and not filter_defender
level: high
source:windows.sysmon @EventID:11 @TargetFilename:(*\mpclient.dll OR *\MpClient.dll OR *\MPCLIENT.DLL) -@TargetFilename:*Defender*
#event_simpleName=FileWritten
| TargetFileName=/\\mpclient\.dll$/i
| NOT (TargetFileName=/Windows Defender/i)
| groupBy([aid, ComputerName, TargetFileName, ContextImageFileName, ContextProcessId], function=count())
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats summariesonly=true count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem where Filesystem.file_name="mpclient.dll" NOT Filesystem.file_path="*\\Windows Defender*" NOT Filesystem.file_path="*\\Windows Defender\\Platform*" by Filesystem.dest Filesystem.file_path Filesystem.file_name Filesystem.process_guid | `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)` | convert ctime(firstTime) ctime(lastTime)
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem where Filesystem.file_name="mpclient.dll" NOT Filesystem.file_path="*\\Windows Defender*" NOT Filesystem.file_path="*\\Windows Defender\\Platform*" by Filesystem.dest Filesystem.file_path Filesystem.file_name Filesystem.process_guid | `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)` | convert ctime(firstTime) ctime(lastTime)
XMRig Monero mining to pool.supportxmr.com / 136.243.203.109 (Vidar drop) AIActions on Objectives Medium
Detects the XMRig payload dropped alongside Vidar reaching out to the campaign's Monero mining pool. Fires on DNS/connection to pool.supportxmr.com or the hard-coded pool IP 136.243.203.109, surfacing the initiating process so an analyst can pivot to the loader. Rationale: pool.supportxmr.com and IP 136.243.203.109 are the article's hard-coded XMRig pool endpoints; contact to a public Monero pool from a corporate endpoint is unauthorized cryptomining with near-zero legitimate use. Fortinet corroborates supportxmr.com:3333 in the same Vidar+XMRig lure. Cross-checked against: • https://www.fortinet.com/blog/threat-research/youtube-pirated-software-videos-deliver-triple-threat-vidar-stealer-laplas-clipper-xmrig-miner • https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1496/
ATT&CKT1496
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Sanctioned/hobbyist Monero mining by a developer on a BYOD host (policy violation, not malware)
  • Threat-intel or IDS appliance sinkholing / test-resolving the pool domain
  • Security researcher detonating a sample in a monitored VM that reports to the same EDR tenant
  • DNS resolver logging cached NXDOMAIN lookups from a browser typo
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe") and InitiatingProcessFolderPath has_any (@"\Downloads\", @"\Temp\", @"\AppData\")
Response runbook
1) TRIAGE: Identify the InitiatingProcess making the connection; a non-browser binary from Downloads/Temp/AppData with high CPU is a strong true positive. 2) CONTAIN: Isolate the host, terminate the miner process, and block 136.243.203.109 and *.supportxmr.com at the egress proxy/firewall. 3) HUNT: On the same host look for the Cluster B mpclient.dll side-load and Vidar credential/cookie/wallet theft; sweep the fleet for the same initiating-process hash and pool contact.
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where RemoteUrl has "supportxmr.com" or RemoteIP == "136.243.203.109"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, RemoteUrl, RemoteIP, RemotePort,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessFolderPath,
          InitiatingProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessSHA256
| order by Timestamp desc
union isfuzzy=true
( ImDnsActivity
  | where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
  | where DnsQuery has "supportxmr.com"
  | project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, SrcIpAddr, Indicator = DnsQuery, Kind = "DNS" ),
( ImNetworkSession
  | where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
  | where DstIpAddr == "136.243.203.109" or DstHostname has "supportxmr.com"
  | project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, SrcIpAddr, Indicator = strcat(DstHostname, " ", DstIpAddr), Kind = "NET" )
| order by TimeGenerated desc
title: XMRig Monero Mining Pool supportxmr.com Contact
id: 2a7e4c15-3d81-4f6b-9c22-7e5a1b8f0d3e
description: Detects DNS resolution of the supportxmr.com Monero mining pool used by the XMRig payload dropped in the Vidar Factory-v3 campaign.
references:
  - https://unit42.paloaltonetworks.com/vidar-stealer-xmrig-miner-campaign-analysis/
author: SOC Detection Engineering
date: 2026/07/08
tags:
  - attack.t1496
  - attack.impact
logsource:
  category: dns
  product: windows
detection:
  selection:
    QueryName|endswith: 'supportxmr.com'
  condition: selection
level: high
source:windows.sysmon @EventID:3 (@DestinationIp:136.243.203.109 OR @DestinationHostname:*supportxmr.com*)
#event_simpleName=DnsRequest
| DomainName=/supportxmr\.com$/i
| groupBy([aid, ComputerName, DomainName, ContextImageFileName, ContextProcessId], function=count())
NETWORK
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats summariesonly=true count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Network_Traffic.All_Traffic where (All_Traffic.dest="136.243.203.109" OR All_Traffic.dest_host="pool.supportxmr.com" OR All_Traffic.dest_host="*.supportxmr.com") by All_Traffic.src All_Traffic.dest All_Traffic.dest_host All_Traffic.dest_port All_Traffic.app | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Traffic)` | convert ctime(firstTime) ctime(lastTime)
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Network_Traffic.All_Traffic where (All_Traffic.dest="136.243.203.109" OR All_Traffic.dest_host="pool.supportxmr.com" OR All_Traffic.dest_host="*.supportxmr.com") by All_Traffic.src All_Traffic.dest All_Traffic.dest_host All_Traffic.dest_port All_Traffic.app | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Traffic)` | convert ctime(firstTime) ctime(lastTime)
Oversized (>100 MB) PE dropped in user path - null-byte file inflation (Vidar loader) AIDelivery Medium
Hunts the Cluster A/C sandbox-evasion trick where the Go loader is inflated to hundreds of megabytes (up to 491 MB) with trailing null bytes to exceed sandbox size limits, while real content is ~2.3 MB. Surfaces abnormally large EXE/DLL files written into Downloads/Temp/AppData. Rationale: Encodes the article's specific evasion measurement: PE files inflated with null-byte padding to as high as 491 MB in user-writable paths. Constraining to EXE/DLL >100 MB in Downloads/Temp/AppData keeps it article-specific rather than a generic large-file alert. Sigma/Datadog/Falcon left empty because their listed schemas don't expose total on-disk file size reliably. Cross-checked against: • https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1027/001/ • https://unit42.paloaltonetworks.com/vidar-stealer-xmrig-miner-campaign-analysis/
ATT&CKT1027.001
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate large game/CAD/media installers downloaded to Downloads
  • Self-extracting archives or bundled runtimes that ship as multi-hundred-MB EXEs
  • Developer build output (large statically-linked binaries) written to a project folder under the user profile
  • Portable VM/emulator images packaged with an .exe wrapper
  • Software-update packages staged in AppData by legitimate updaters
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("msiexec.exe","setup.exe","steam.exe","epicgameslauncher.exe","onedrive.exe") and InitiatingProcessFileName has_any ("7z","winrar","rar","unzip","explorer")
Response runbook
1) TRIAGE: Check the file's real vs. padded size (a ~2.4 MB compressed size against a 400 MB+ on-disk file is the tell) and the writing process; download origin from a cracked-software domain is a strong positive. 2) CONTAIN: Quarantine the file, isolate the host if it also executed, and submit a de-padded copy to sandbox/AV. 3) HUNT: Pivot on the initiating process and SHA256; look for subsequent mpclient.dll side-load and supportxmr.com egress indicating the full Vidar+XMRig chain.
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where ActionType == "FileCreated"
| where FileName endswith ".exe" or FileName endswith ".dll"
| where FileSize > 104857600   // 100 MB; article loaders reached 491 MB, real content only ~2.3 MB
| where FolderPath has_any (@"\Downloads\", @"\Temp\", @"\AppData\")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, FileName, FolderPath, FileSize, SHA256,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFolderPath
| order by FileSize desc
ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where EventType == "FileCreated"
| where TargetFileExtension in~ ("exe","dll")
| where TargetFileSize > 104857600   // 100 MB inflation threshold; article samples up to 491 MB
| where TargetFilePath has_any (@"\Downloads\", @"\Temp\", @"\AppData\")
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, TargetFilePath, TargetFileSize, TargetFileSHA256,
          ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine
| order by TargetFileSize desc
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats summariesonly=true count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem where (Filesystem.file_name="*.exe" OR Filesystem.file_name="*.dll") Filesystem.file_size>104857600 (Filesystem.file_path="*\\Downloads\\*" OR Filesystem.file_path="*\\Temp\\*" OR Filesystem.file_path="*\\AppData\\*") by Filesystem.dest Filesystem.file_path Filesystem.file_name Filesystem.file_size Filesystem.process_guid | `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)` | convert ctime(firstTime) ctime(lastTime) | sort - file_size
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem where (Filesystem.file_name="*.exe" OR Filesystem.file_name="*.dll") Filesystem.file_size>104857600 (Filesystem.file_path="*\\Downloads\\*" OR Filesystem.file_path="*\\Temp\\*" OR Filesystem.file_path="*\\AppData\\*") by Filesystem.dest Filesystem.file_path Filesystem.file_name Filesystem.file_size Filesystem.process_guid | `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)` | convert ctime(firstTime) ctime(lastTime) | sort - file_size
Beaconing — periodic outbound to small set of destinations Command & Control Medium
C2 channel detection via inter-beacon-time stddev / fan-out to single dest.
ATT&CKT1071.001 T1071.004
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic DeviceNetworkEvents
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where RemoteIPType == "Public" and ActionType == "ConnectionSuccess"
| project DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort, Timestamp
| sort by DeviceName asc, RemoteIP asc, RemotePort asc, Timestamp asc
| extend prev_dev = prev(DeviceName, 1), prev_ip = prev(RemoteIP, 1),
         prev_port = prev(RemotePort, 1), prev_ts = prev(Timestamp, 1)
| where DeviceName == prev_dev and RemoteIP == prev_ip and RemotePort == prev_port
| extend delta_sec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, prev_ts)
| summarize conn_count = count(), avg_delta = avg(delta_sec), stdev_delta = stdev(delta_sec)
    by DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort
| where conn_count > 30 and avg_delta between (30.0 .. 600.0) and stdev_delta < 5.0
| order by conn_count desc
ImNetworkSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(2h)
| where DvcAction != "Block"
| where ipv4_is_private(DstIpAddr) == false
| summarize ConnCount = count(),
            DistinctMinutes = dcount(bin(TimeGenerated, 1m))
            by DvcHostname, DstIpAddr, DstPortNumber
| where ConnCount > 50 and DistinctMinutes > 30   // sustained, not bursty
| order by ConnCount desc
NETWORK
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count, values(All_Traffic.dest_port) AS ports
    from datamodel=Network_Traffic.All_Traffic
    where All_Traffic.action="allowed" AND All_Traffic.dest_category!="internal"
    by _time span=10s, All_Traffic.src, All_Traffic.dest
| `drop_dm_object_name(All_Traffic)`
| streamstats current=f last(_time) AS prev_time by src, dest
| eval delta = _time - prev_time
| stats avg(delta) AS avg_delta stdev(delta) AS sd_delta count by src, dest
| where count > 30 AND sd_delta < 5 AND avg_delta>=30 AND avg_delta<=600
| sort - count
| tstats summariesonly=false count, values(All_Traffic.dest_port) AS ports
    from datamodel=Network_Traffic.All_Traffic
    where All_Traffic.action="allowed" AND All_Traffic.dest_category!="internal"
    by _time span=10s, All_Traffic.src, All_Traffic.dest
| `drop_dm_object_name(All_Traffic)`
| streamstats current=f last(_time) AS prev_time by src, dest
| eval delta = _time - prev_time
| stats avg(delta) AS avg_delta stdev(delta) AS sd_delta count by src, dest
| where count > 30 AND sd_delta < 5 AND avg_delta>=30 AND avg_delta<=600
| sort - count

Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution Delivery High
User received an external email containing a URL, clicked it, and within 60 seconds the recipient's endpoint spawned a scripting interpreter or network downloader (PowerShell / cmd / mshta / curl / certutil / bitsadmin). This is the high-fidelity shape — a raw "user clicked an emailed URL" query is too noisy to alert on because every Microsoft 365 tenant generates thousands of legitimate clicks per day. The exec-correlation step suppresses the noise to roughly the rate at which a click actually drives onto-host execution, which is the actionable signal. Pair with UC_PHISH_LINK_BYPASS (Safe Links override) and UC_PHISH_LINK_NEWDOMAIN for orthogonal high-fidelity variants.
ATT&CKT1566.002 T1204.001 T1059.001
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Web Endpoint.Processes EmailEvents EmailUrlInfo UrlClickEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s.
// Far higher fidelity than "every clicked URL" — most legitimate clicks
// never spawn a non-browser child process, so the join eliminates the
// 99% of noise that makes a raw click query unactionable.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectClicks = UrlClickEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | where ActionType in ("ClickAllowed","ClickedThrough")
    | join kind=inner (
        EmailEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
        | where DeliveryAction == "Delivered"
        | where EmailDirection == "Inbound"
        | project NetworkMessageId, Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain,
                  RecipientEmailAddress, EmailTimestamp = Timestamp
      ) on NetworkMessageId
    | join kind=leftouter (
        EmailUrlInfo | project NetworkMessageId, Url, UrlDomain
      ) on NetworkMessageId, Url
    | project ClickTime = Timestamp, AccountUpn, IPAddress, Url, UrlDomain,
              Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain, RecipientEmailAddress,
              ActionType;
// Correlate to a non-browser child process spawned within 60 seconds on
// the recipient's device.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                         "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                        "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                        "bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe","curl.exe","wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectClicks on $left.AccountName == $right.AccountUpn
| where Timestamp between (ClickTime .. ClickTime + 60s)
| project ClickTime, ProcessTime = Timestamp,
          DelaySec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, ClickTime),
          DeviceName, AccountName, RecipientEmailAddress, SenderFromAddress,
          Subject, Url, UrlDomain, ActionType,
          FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by ClickTime desc
// UrlClickEvents has no clean Sentinel-native equivalent. The detection
// pivots to: Office Send→Receive proximity to SecurityEvent 4688 of a
// non-browser child process. Lower fidelity than the Defender version.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectMailUsers = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation =~ "Receive"
    | summarize Subject = any(Subject), Sender = any(Sender)
                by MailboxOwnerUPN, MessageId, EmailTime = bin(TimeGenerated, 1m);
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("\chrome.exe","\msedge.exe",
                                     "\firefox.exe","\outlook.exe","\brave.exe")
| where NewProcessName has_any ("\powershell.exe","\pwsh.exe","\cmd.exe",
                                  "\mshta.exe","\rundll32.exe","\regsvr32.exe",
                                  "\wscript.exe","\cscript.exe","\bitsadmin.exe",
                                  "\certutil.exe","\curl.exe","\wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectMailUsers on $left.Account == $right.MailboxOwnerUPN
| where TimeGenerated between (EmailTime .. EmailTime + 60s)
| project TimeGenerated, EmailTime, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName,
          NewProcessName, CommandLine, Sender, Subject
| order by TimeGenerated desc
WEB
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"
    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| rename user AS recipient, dest AS clicked_domain, url AS clicked_url
| join type=inner recipient
    [| tstats `summariesonly` count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"
         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"
     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",
                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
     | rename dest AS src]
| eval delta_sec = exec_time - click_time
| where delta_sec >= 0 AND delta_sec <= 60
| table click_time, exec_time, delta_sec, recipient, src, src_user, subject,
        clicked_domain, clicked_url, exec_proc, exec_cmd
| sort - click_time

Better-auth refresh_token grant to /oauth2/token or /mcp/token missing client authentication (CVE-2026-53512) AIExploitation Medium
Hunts POST requests to better-auth's legacy token endpoints (/api/auth/oauth2/token, /api/auth/mcp/token) that carry no Authorization: Basic header yet succeed (HTTP 200). Because the vulnerable refresh_token grant never verifies a confidential client's client_secret, a successful, unauthenticated token mint on these exact paths is the direct exploitation signature of CVE-2026-53512/53513. Rationale: Uses the two exact vulnerable endpoint paths named in the advisory plus the missing Authorization header (client_secret is passed via Authorization: Basic on the auth-code grant), which is the precise omission on the refresh path. Endpoint paths corroborated against Better Auth's official mcp/oidc-provider docs. Cross-checked against: • https://better-auth.com/docs/plugins/mcp • https://better-auth.com/docs/plugins/oidc-provider • https://better-auth.com/docs/plugins/oauth-provider
ATT&CKT1550.001 T1212 T1078
Data sourcesWeb.Web
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate PUBLIC (PKCE) clients calling the token endpoint — they correctly carry no client_secret and are not vulnerable
  • Server-to-server confidential clients that (mis)send credentials in the request body instead of the Authorization header, which some logging pipelines strip
  • Load-balancer or WAF that terminates TLS and drops/normalizes the Authorization header before the log stage
  • Health-check or uptime probes POSTing to the token endpoint
  • Native mobile clients registered as public performing normal refresh
Suppression filter
| where not(HttpRequestHeaderUserAgent has_any ("HealthCheck","Pingdom","UptimeRobot","kube-probe"))
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm the target app runs better-auth < 1.6.11 with oidcProvider() or mcp() enabled and has at least one confidential client (oauthApplication type web/native/user-agent-based). Pull the SrcIpAddr, User-Agent and whether the client_id maps to a confidential client. 2) Contain: upgrade to better-auth@1.6.11+ (or migrate to @better-auth/oauth-provider); as an immediate stop-gap run db.deleteMany on oauthAccessToken for the affected clientId to revoke all refresh chains, and restrict the two token paths to known client IPs at the LB. 3) Hunt: pivot on the returned SrcIpAddr/User-Agent for other successful token mints (UC3) and correlate downstream resource-server API calls bearing the minted access tokens for the impersonated user's scope.
ImWebSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where Url has_any ("/api/auth/oauth2/token", "/api/auth/mcp/token")
| where HttpMethod =~ "POST"
| where HttpStatusCode == 200
| where isempty(HttpRequestHeaderAuthorization)   // no confidential-client credential presented, yet token minted = CVE-2026-53512 refresh bypass
| project TimeGenerated, SrcIpAddr, DstHostname, Url, HttpMethod, HttpStatusCode, HttpRequestHeaderUserAgent, HttpRequestHeaderReferer
| order by TimeGenerated desc
WEB

Cross-origin browser request to better-auth /mcp/token abusing wildcard CORS (CVE-2026-53513) AIDelivery Medium
Hunts requests to /api/auth/mcp/token whose Referer/Origin host does not match the application's own host, indicating a cross-origin script pulling tokens. The mcp endpoint shipped Access-Control-Allow-Origin: * unconditionally (fixed in 1.6.11), which amplifies the refresh bypass into a browser-side token-harvest vector. Rationale: Targets the specific mcp token path plus a Referer-host vs target-host mismatch, the exact browser-context abuse the advisory calls out (wildcard Access-Control-Allow-Origin:* amplifying the refresh bypass). High-signal because same-origin app traffic to its own token endpoint should never carry a foreign Referer host. Cross-checked against: • https://better-auth.com/docs/plugins/mcp • https://better-auth.com/docs/plugins/oauth-provider
ATT&CKT1528 T1550.001
Data sourcesWeb.Web
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate multi-domain deployments where the SPA is served from a different hostname than the auth API (e.g. app.example.com calling auth.example.com)
  • CDN/edge hostnames rewriting the observed DstHostname so it never equals the Referer host
  • Browser extensions or corporate proxies that strip or rewrite the Referer header
  • Marketing/redirect domains that legitimately front the auth API
  • Mobile webviews presenting an app-scheme Referer
Suppression filter
| where RefererHost !endswith "example.com"   // replace example.com with your first-party auth/app domain suffix to suppress legit cross-subdomain SPA traffic
Response runbook
1) Triage: resolve RefererHost — is it a domain you own/allowlist, or an attacker-controlled site? Check whether the response actually carried Access-Control-Allow-Origin:* (mcp endpoint pre-1.6.11) and whether the call returned 200. 2) Contain: drop the wildcard CORS at an upstream proxy and replace with a tight allowlist for /api/auth/mcp/token; upgrade to 1.6.11+. If RefererHost is hostile, revoke refresh tokens for affected clients via oauthAccessToken deleteMany. 3) Hunt: sweep for the same RefererHost across all endpoints, and pivot the SrcIpAddr into UC1/UC3 to see if the harvested tokens were then replayed against the token endpoint.
ImWebSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where Url has "/api/auth/mcp/token"
| where isnotempty(HttpRequestHeaderReferer)
| extend RefererHost = tostring(parse_url(HttpRequestHeaderReferer).Host)
| extend TargetHost = tostring(coalesce(DstHostname, DvcHostname))
| where isnotempty(RefererHost) and isnotempty(TargetHost) and RefererHost != TargetHost
| project TimeGenerated, SrcIpAddr, TargetHost, RefererHost, Url, HttpMethod, HttpStatusCode, HttpRequestHeaderUserAgent
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count, values(Web.http_user_agent) as user_agents, min(_time) as firstTime, max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Web where Web.uri_path="/api/auth/mcp/token" Web.http_referrer=* by Web.src, Web.dest, Web.http_referrer, Web.uri_path | `drop_dm_object_name(Web)` | rex field=http_referrer "^https?://(?<referrer_host>[^/:]+)" | where referrer_host!=dest | sort - count | `security_content_ctime(firstTime)` | `security_content_ctime(lastTime)`
| tstats summariesonly=false count, values(Web.http_user_agent) as user_agents, min(_time) as firstTime, max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Web where Web.uri_path="/api/auth/mcp/token" Web.http_referrer=* by Web.src, Web.dest, Web.http_referrer, Web.uri_path | `drop_dm_object_name(Web)` | rex field=http_referrer "^https?://(?<referrer_host>[^/:]+)" | where referrer_host!=dest | sort - count | `security_content_ctime(firstTime)` | `security_content_ctime(lastTime)`
Sustained refresh-token minting from a new source IP against better-auth token endpoint (rotation persistence) AIInstallation Medium
Alerts when a source IP not seen in the prior 14-day baseline produces a burst of successful (HTTP 200) POSTs to /api/auth/oauth2/token or /api/auth/mcp/token. Token rotation re-issues a refresh_token and resets the 7-day window each call, so an attacker holding one leaked refresh_token drives a steady cadence of grants from a fixed new IP to maintain indefinite impersonation. Rationale: Combines the two exact vulnerable endpoint paths, successful-mint filter (status 200 + POST), a 14-day new-IP baseline anti-join, and a repetition threshold to model the article's core persistence mechanic (rotation resets the 7-day window each call). New IP + repeated successful grants is the automation fingerprint of an attacker keeping a leaked chain alive. Cross-checked against: • https://better-auth.com/docs/plugins/mcp • https://better-auth.com/docs/plugins/oidc-provider
ATT&CKT1550.001 T1078 T1606
Data sourcesWeb.Web
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • A legitimate new backend/service instance or autoscaled worker coming online with a fresh egress IP and refreshing tokens on schedule
  • Corporate VPN/NAT egress IP rotation bringing a 'new' IP that is really existing users
  • A newly deployed mobile app version or SDK bump changing the refresh cadence
  • CI/CD or integration-test runners exercising the OAuth flow from ephemeral cloud IPs
  • Legitimate SSO migration that re-issues many tokens in a short window
Suppression filter
| where SrcIpAddr !in ("")   // populate with your known service/NAT/CI egress IPs to suppress first-party automation
Response runbook
1) Triage: is the new SrcIpAddr attributable to your own infra (autoscale, VPN, CI)? Check the associated client_id — is it a confidential client, and does the geo/ASN of the IP match the legitimate user's baseline? 2) Contain: if unattributed, revoke the client's refresh chain (db.deleteMany on oauthAccessToken where clientId), upgrade to better-auth@1.6.11+, and IP-restrict the token endpoints at the LB. 3) Hunt: correlate the minted access tokens forward to resource-server activity for scope-level reads/writes that diverge from the user's normal pattern, and back-check UC1/UC2 for how the refresh_token was originally leaked (missing-auth POST or cross-origin CORS pull).
let Lookback = 14d;
let Recent = 1d;
let KnownIps = ImWebSession
    | where TimeGenerated between (ago(Lookback + Recent) .. ago(Recent))
    | where Url has_any ("/api/auth/oauth2/token", "/api/auth/mcp/token")
    | summarize by SrcIpAddr;
ImWebSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(Recent)
| where Url has_any ("/api/auth/oauth2/token", "/api/auth/mcp/token")
| where HttpMethod =~ "POST" and HttpStatusCode == 200
| join kind=leftanti KnownIps on SrcIpAddr
| summarize TokenCalls = count(), FirstSeen = min(TimeGenerated), LastSeen = max(TimeGenerated), Endpoints = make_set(Url), UserAgents = make_set(HttpRequestHeaderUserAgent) by SrcIpAddr
| where TokenCalls >= 5   // 5 = sustained rotation cadence: >=5 successful token grants in 24h from a brand-new source IP
| order by TokenCalls desc

UAT-7810 targeted n-day CVE exposure on internet-facing Ruckus/ASUS edge devices AIExploitation Medium
Surfaces managed devices carrying the exact Ruckus and ASUS AiCloud router CVEs UAT-7810 exploits for initial access (CVE-2020-22653, CVE-2020-22658, CVE-2023-25717, CVE-2025-2492), prioritising internet-facing assets. This is an attack-surface hunt tied to the specific n-days named in the Talos campaign, not a generic vuln report. Rationale: Uses the four CVE IDs Talos explicitly attributes to UAT-7810's initial access against Ruckus and ASUS AiCloud routers; scoping to IsInternetFacing devices makes exposure high-fidelity for surface reduction. Cross-checked against: • https://www.bleepingcomputer.com/news/security/chinese-hackers-develop-longleash-malware-to-expand-orb-network/ • https://cloud.google.com/blog/topics/threat-intelligence/orb-networks-hide-china-espionage
ATT&CKT1190
Data sourcesVulnerabilities.Vulnerabilities
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimately vulnerable-but-segmented lab/test routers flagged as internet-facing by NAT misclassification
  • Devices already scheduled for patching in the current maintenance window
  • Vendor virtual appliances that share a CPE string with the affected Ruckus/ASUS models
  • Decommissioned edge devices still reporting inventory before removal
Response runbook
Step 1 (triage): Confirm the device is genuinely internet-reachable on its management/AiCloud service and record firmware version vs the fixed build for each CVE. Step 2 (contain): Restrict management-plane exposure (ACL/VPN-only) and schedule emergency firmware update; where patching is blocked, disable AiCloud/remote admin. Step 3 (hunt): Pivot to UC4 to check whether the device has beaconed to the ORB relay IPs, and inspect the router for unexpected listening ports and web-root scripts (DOGLEASH).

Web server spawning shell/listener on Linux edge host (DOGLEASH web-shell deployment) AIInstallation Medium
Hunts a web server or PHP process spawning an interactive shell, netcat, or interpreter on Linux/IoT hosts — the execution chain Talos describes for DOGLEASH, a lightweight Linux backdoor 'deployed via web shell scripts' that opens a listening TCP port. Targets the router/Linux appliance execution surface, not generic Office macro chains. Rationale: Anchors on Talos's specific description of DOGLEASH being 'deployed via web shell scripts' with 'shell command execution' and opening a listening TCP port; a web-server parent spawning shell/nc on Linux edge devices is the article's execution fingerprint. Cross-checked against: • https://www.bleepingcomputer.com/news/security/chinese-hackers-develop-longleash-malware-to-expand-orb-network/
ATT&CKT1505.003 T1059.004
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • PHP/CGI applications that legitimately shell out to sh for image processing or backups
  • Monitoring agents (Nagios/Zabbix) invoking check scripts under the web user
  • CI/CD or webhook handlers spawning python/perl build steps
  • Cron-invoked maintenance scripts parented to a lingering php-fpm worker
Suppression filter
| where ProcessCommandLine has_any ("/dev/tcp/","-e /bin/sh","-e /bin/bash","bash -i","nc -l","ncat -l","socket","pty.spawn")
Response runbook
Step 1 (triage): Inspect the child command line — decode any base64, look for reverse-shell (/dev/tcp, nc -l, -e /bin/sh) or listener setup, and identify the writing process's web root. Step 2 (contain): Isolate the host from egress, kill the listener, and preserve the web-accessible directory for the dropped web-shell script. Step 3 (hunt): Enumerate listening TCP ports on the device (UC covers the hardcoded-password listener), sweep for the UAT-7810 file hashes (UC3), and check for outbound relay to the ORB IPs (UC4).

| where AccountName !endswith "$"

UAT-7810 LONGLEASH/DOGLEASH malware sample hash on endpoint AIInstallation Medium
Alerts on any file or process matching the SHA256 hashes Talos published for the UAT-7810 toolset (LONGLEASH, DOGLEASH, JARLEASH, LEASHTEST). Direct IOC match against the campaign's confirmed samples. Rationale: Direct SHA256 IOC match against the six hashes Talos attributes to the UAT-7810 toolset; exact-hash matches are the highest-fidelity signal available for this campaign. Cross-checked against: • https://www.bleepingcomputer.com/news/security/chinese-hackers-develop-longleash-malware-to-expand-orb-network/ • https://cloud.google.com/blog/topics/threat-intelligence/orb-networks-hide-china-espionage
ATT&CKT1105 T1505.003
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Malware analyst or sandbox host intentionally holding the sample for research
  • EDR/AV quarantine copy of the sample generating a secondary file event
  • Threat-intel platform caching the binary during automated enrichment
  • Backup/imaging job re-reading a previously infected volume
Suppression filter
| where not (DeviceName has_any ("sandbox","malware","reverse","detonation"))
Response runbook
Step 1 (triage): Confirm the hash and identify the host, the writing process, and file path; determine if the host is a sanctioned analysis/sandbox machine. Step 2 (contain): Isolate the endpoint, block the hash org-wide, and preserve the binary for reverse engineering. Step 3 (hunt): Pivot to the same host's network events for ORB relay IP contact (UC4), enumerate listening ports for the hardcoded-password backdoor, and hash-sweep the fleet for the remaining toolset samples.

UAT-7810 ORB relay node communication (LONGLEASH C2 infrastructure IPs) AICommand & Control Medium
Alerts on any inbound or outbound traffic to the four UAT-7810 ORB relay/C2 IPs published by Talos, which LONGLEASH uses for multi-protocol proxying and intermediate-C2 forwarding. Direct network IOC match against the campaign's confirmed relay infrastructure. Rationale: Direct match on the four ORB relay/C2 IPs Talos ties to UAT-7810/LONGLEASH; any internal host or edge device contacting these addresses is a high-confidence relay-node or C2 indicator. Cross-checked against: • https://www.bleepingcomputer.com/news/security/chinese-hackers-develop-longleash-malware-to-expand-orb-network/ • https://cloud.google.com/blog/topics/threat-intelligence/orb-networks-hide-china-espionage
ATT&CKT1090.003 T1090.001 T1572 T1071.004
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Security appliance actively scanning/validating the IPs against a blocklist
  • Threat-intel enrichment platform test-connecting to the indicator
  • Shared-hosting IP reassigned to a benign service after Talos publication
  • Researcher sandbox detonating the sample and reaching the live C2
Response runbook
Step 1 (triage): Identify the internal host/edge device and the process/interface generating the traffic, and the protocol/port (watch for DNS/ICMP/SOCKS tunneling and TLS with self-signed PKI). Step 2 (contain): Block the four IPs at the perimeter, isolate the source device, and capture full-packet or netflow for the session. Step 3 (hunt): Determine whether the device is an ingress relay (inbound from the IPs) or egress node, sweep the fleet for the toolset hashes (UC3), and check the same host for the web-shell execution chain (UC2) and unauthorized listening ports.
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where RemoteIP in ("194.233.92.26","217.15.160.247","217.15.164.147","95.182.100.231")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, DeviceId, ActionType, RemoteIP, RemotePort, Protocol, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFolderPath
| order by Timestamp desc

| where DestinationIP in ("194.233.92.26","217.15.160.247","217.15.164.147","95.182.100.231")
   or SourceIP in ("194.233.92.26","217.15.160.247","217.15.164.147","95.182.100.231")
| project TimeGenerated, DeviceVendor, DeviceProduct, SourceIP, SourcePort, DestinationIP, DestinationPort, ApplicationProtocol, DeviceAction
| order by TimeGenerated desc
title: UAT-7810 ORB Relay Node C2 Communication
id: c1a7f3d8-5e42-49b6-8f30-2b9d6c4a71e2

description: Detects network connections to Cisco Talos published UAT-7810 ORB relay/C2 IP addresses used by LONGLEASH for proxying and intermediate C2.
references:

  - attack.t1572

Beaconing — periodic outbound to small set of destinations Command & Control Medium
C2 channel detection via inter-beacon-time stddev / fan-out to single dest.
ATT&CKT1071.001 T1071.004
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic DeviceNetworkEvents
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where RemoteIPType == "Public" and ActionType == "ConnectionSuccess"
| project DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort, Timestamp
| sort by DeviceName asc, RemoteIP asc, RemotePort asc, Timestamp asc
| extend prev_dev = prev(DeviceName, 1), prev_ip = prev(RemoteIP, 1),
         prev_port = prev(RemotePort, 1), prev_ts = prev(Timestamp, 1)
| where DeviceName == prev_dev and RemoteIP == prev_ip and RemotePort == prev_port
| extend delta_sec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, prev_ts)
| summarize conn_count = count(), avg_delta = avg(delta_sec), stdev_delta = stdev(delta_sec)
    by DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort
| where conn_count > 30 and avg_delta between (30.0 .. 600.0) and stdev_delta < 5.0
| order by conn_count desc
ImNetworkSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(2h)
| where DvcAction != "Block"
| where ipv4_is_private(DstIpAddr) == false
| summarize ConnCount = count(),
            DistinctMinutes = dcount(bin(TimeGenerated, 1m))
            by DvcHostname, DstIpAddr, DstPortNumber
| where ConnCount > 50 and DistinctMinutes > 30   // sustained, not bursty
| order by ConnCount desc
NETWORK
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count, values(All_Traffic.dest_port) AS ports
    from datamodel=Network_Traffic.All_Traffic
    where All_Traffic.action="allowed" AND All_Traffic.dest_category!="internal"
    by _time span=10s, All_Traffic.src, All_Traffic.dest
| `drop_dm_object_name(All_Traffic)`
| streamstats current=f last(_time) AS prev_time by src, dest
| eval delta = _time - prev_time
| stats avg(delta) AS avg_delta stdev(delta) AS sd_delta count by src, dest
| where count > 30 AND sd_delta < 5 AND avg_delta>=30 AND avg_delta<=600
| sort - count
| tstats summariesonly=false count, values(All_Traffic.dest_port) AS ports
    from datamodel=Network_Traffic.All_Traffic
    where All_Traffic.action="allowed" AND All_Traffic.dest_category!="internal"
    by _time span=10s, All_Traffic.src, All_Traffic.dest
| `drop_dm_object_name(All_Traffic)`
| streamstats current=f last(_time) AS prev_time by src, dest
| eval delta = _time - prev_time
| stats avg(delta) AS avg_delta stdev(delta) AS sd_delta count by src, dest
| where count > 30 AND sd_delta < 5 AND avg_delta>=30 AND avg_delta<=600
| sort - count
Network connections to article IPs / domains Command & Control High
Outbound traffic to attacker infrastructure named in the article.
ATT&CKT1071
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic Web Network_Resolution.DNS DeviceNetworkEvents
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where RemoteIP in ("194.233.92.26", "217.15.160.247", "217.15.164.147", "95.182.100.231") or RemoteUrl has_any ("")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, RemoteIP, RemotePort, RemoteUrl,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine
let BadIPs     = dynamic(["194.233.92.26", "217.15.160.247", "217.15.164.147", "95.182.100.231"]);
let BadDomains = dynamic([""]);
ImNetworkSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where DstIpAddr in (BadIPs)
   or Url has_any (BadDomains)
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, DstIpAddr, DstPortNumber, Url, NetworkProtocol
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Asset exposure — vulnerability matches article CVE(s) Reconnaissance High
Match vulnerability scanner output to the CVE(s) named in the article.
ATT&CKT1190
Data sourcesVulnerabilities DeviceInfo DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities
// TVM tables are daily snapshots — pin a 1-day window so the engine
// partitions on Timestamp instead of scanning the full retention.
DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where CveId in~ ("CVE-2020-22653", "CVE-2020-22658", "CVE-2023-25717", "CVE-2025-2492")
| join kind=inner (DeviceInfo | where Timestamp > ago(1d)) on DeviceId
| project DeviceName, OSPlatform, CveId, VulnerabilitySeverityLevel, RecommendedSecurityUpdate
| order by VulnerabilitySeverityLevel asc, DeviceName asc

// Sentinel has no native TVM table. If MDE→Sentinel streaming is enabled,
// `DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities` is available. Otherwise this UC has
// no Sentinel translation — track via Update / Heartbeat OS-version
// gaps as a coarse approximation.
DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities
| where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)
| where CveId in~ ("CVE-2020-22653", "CVE-2020-22658", "CVE-2023-25717", "CVE-2025-2492")
| join kind=inner (DeviceInfo | where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)) on DeviceId
| project DeviceName, OSPlatform, CveId,
          VulnerabilitySeverityLevel, RecommendedSecurityUpdate
| order by VulnerabilitySeverityLevel asc, DeviceName asc

File hash IOCs — endpoint file/process match Installation High
Match SHA256/SHA1/MD5 named in the article against EDR file/process telemetry.
ATT&CKT1027
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem Endpoint.Processes DeviceFileEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Pre-filter each table BEFORE the union — the engine cannot push
// predicates across `union`, and DeviceFileEvents lacks ProcessCommandLine
// (Initiating only) so column-projection has to differ per side.
union
    ( DeviceFileEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(7d)
        | where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ ("1b5649b479fd625de5c8120873644b5eb669cc89cd504582c18e0ae350fd8823", "755fcee1337a252203002ecfdf673a08cfadeda8d738bef2d518a08e0626aa4f", "324d95024fc8da5c92b5a1f4825aed5a2a91c9ca8fb6aa52abb332a4c9cf4257", "bafba443170e54ef7fd431ce7f1b5e202719f3fd022e4ef70788904f574d2cdf", "e799d72929d7ccc7f6b6109742b8cc482838303207efc989543b6e1ca6d16e9c", "3b89d183eb014e29d9d0d4e45fc2b784a7fcfcf31dd48fd3bde30f8d956383d1") or SHA1 in~ ("1b5649b479fd625de5c8120873644b5eb669cc89cd504582c18e0ae350fd8823", "755fcee1337a252203002ecfdf673a08cfadeda8d738bef2d518a08e0626aa4f", "324d95024fc8da5c92b5a1f4825aed5a2a91c9ca8fb6aa52abb332a4c9cf4257", "bafba443170e54ef7fd431ce7f1b5e202719f3fd022e4ef70788904f574d2cdf", "e799d72929d7ccc7f6b6109742b8cc482838303207efc989543b6e1ca6d16e9c", "3b89d183eb014e29d9d0d4e45fc2b784a7fcfcf31dd48fd3bde30f8d956383d1") or MD5 in~ ("1b5649b479fd625de5c8120873644b5eb669cc89cd504582c18e0ae350fd8823", "755fcee1337a252203002ecfdf673a08cfadeda8d738bef2d518a08e0626aa4f", "324d95024fc8da5c92b5a1f4825aed5a2a91c9ca8fb6aa52abb332a4c9cf4257", "bafba443170e54ef7fd431ce7f1b5e202719f3fd022e4ef70788904f574d2cdf", "e799d72929d7ccc7f6b6109742b8cc482838303207efc989543b6e1ca6d16e9c", "3b89d183eb014e29d9d0d4e45fc2b784a7fcfcf31dd48fd3bde30f8d956383d1")
        | project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256,
                  Cmd = InitiatingProcessCommandLine, Source = "DeviceFileEvents" ),
    ( DeviceProcessEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(7d)
        | where AccountName !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ ("1b5649b479fd625de5c8120873644b5eb669cc89cd504582c18e0ae350fd8823", "755fcee1337a252203002ecfdf673a08cfadeda8d738bef2d518a08e0626aa4f", "324d95024fc8da5c92b5a1f4825aed5a2a91c9ca8fb6aa52abb332a4c9cf4257", "bafba443170e54ef7fd431ce7f1b5e202719f3fd022e4ef70788904f574d2cdf", "e799d72929d7ccc7f6b6109742b8cc482838303207efc989543b6e1ca6d16e9c", "3b89d183eb014e29d9d0d4e45fc2b784a7fcfcf31dd48fd3bde30f8d956383d1") or SHA1 in~ ("1b5649b479fd625de5c8120873644b5eb669cc89cd504582c18e0ae350fd8823", "755fcee1337a252203002ecfdf673a08cfadeda8d738bef2d518a08e0626aa4f", "324d95024fc8da5c92b5a1f4825aed5a2a91c9ca8fb6aa52abb332a4c9cf4257", "bafba443170e54ef7fd431ce7f1b5e202719f3fd022e4ef70788904f574d2cdf", "e799d72929d7ccc7f6b6109742b8cc482838303207efc989543b6e1ca6d16e9c", "3b89d183eb014e29d9d0d4e45fc2b784a7fcfcf31dd48fd3bde30f8d956383d1") or MD5 in~ ("1b5649b479fd625de5c8120873644b5eb669cc89cd504582c18e0ae350fd8823", "755fcee1337a252203002ecfdf673a08cfadeda8d738bef2d518a08e0626aa4f", "324d95024fc8da5c92b5a1f4825aed5a2a91c9ca8fb6aa52abb332a4c9cf4257", "bafba443170e54ef7fd431ce7f1b5e202719f3fd022e4ef70788904f574d2cdf", "e799d72929d7ccc7f6b6109742b8cc482838303207efc989543b6e1ca6d16e9c", "3b89d183eb014e29d9d0d4e45fc2b784a7fcfcf31dd48fd3bde30f8d956383d1")
        | project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256,
                  Cmd = ProcessCommandLine, Source = "DeviceProcessEvents" )
| order by Timestamp desc

// Pre-filter both ASIM tables before the union — same pattern as the
// Defender version so the engine can push hash predicates per-side.
let BadHashes = dynamic(["1b5649b479fd625de5c8120873644b5eb669cc89cd504582c18e0ae350fd8823", "755fcee1337a252203002ecfdf673a08cfadeda8d738bef2d518a08e0626aa4f", "324d95024fc8da5c92b5a1f4825aed5a2a91c9ca8fb6aa52abb332a4c9cf4257", "bafba443170e54ef7fd431ce7f1b5e202719f3fd022e4ef70788904f574d2cdf", "e799d72929d7ccc7f6b6109742b8cc482838303207efc989543b6e1ca6d16e9c", "3b89d183eb014e29d9d0d4e45fc2b784a7fcfcf31dd48fd3bde30f8d956383d1"]);
union
    ( ImFileEvent
        | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
        | where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
        | where TargetFileSHA256 in~ (BadHashes)
           or TargetFileSHA1 in~ (BadHashes)
           or TargetFileMD5 in~ (BadHashes)
        | project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, EventType,
                  TargetFileName, TargetFilePath, TargetFileSHA256,
                  Cmd = ActingProcessName, Source = "ImFileEvent" ),
    ( ImProcessCreate
        | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
        | where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ (BadHashes) or SHA1 in~ (BadHashes) or MD5 in~ (BadHashes)
        | project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, EventType = TargetProcessName,
                  TargetFileName = TargetProcessName, TargetFilePath = TargetProcessName,
                  TargetFileSHA256 = SHA256,
                  Cmd = TargetProcessCommandLine, Source = "ImProcessCreate" )
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Critical

RedWing MaaS Packages Android Bank Fraud as a Telegram Rental Service

The Hacker News
2026-07-07 11 use cases 6 techniques 5 kill-chain phases detected

A new Android malware operation called RedWing is being rented out on Telegram as a ready-made bank-fraud service. It lets even low-skill criminals take over a victim's phone, steal their banking logins, and capture the one-time codes that protect their accounts. Zimperium's zLabs, which found the operation, says it looks like a new variant of Oblivion, a $300-a-month rent-a-malware tool

ATT&CKT1190 T1204.002 T1486 T1555.003 T1566 T1566.002

Actions on Objectives
Detected
Reconnaissance. Attacker researches the target — OSINT, scanning, enumeration.
Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad). → [LLM] RedWing Android MaaS: fake-store APK delivery infrastructure contact · Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution · Email attachment opened from external sender
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code. → Office app spawning script/LOLBin child process · Fake CAPTCHA / clipboard-injected PowerShell (ClickFix / FakeCaptcha)
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key. → Suspicious browser extension installation
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking. → [LLM] RedWing Android banking trojan C2 beacon (krusty-crabs.sbs / redwing.top / workers.dev)
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage. → Infostealer — non-browser process accessing browser cookie/login DBs · Ransomware-style mass file rename / extension change · LSASS process access / dump (credential theft) · Remote service execution — PsExec / SMB lateral movement
RedWing Android MaaS: fake-store APK delivery infrastructure contact AIDelivery High
Hunts network connections to the RedWing dropper distribution hosts and the trojanized Proton VPN APK URL that Zimperium tied to this Telegram-rented Android bank-fraud kit. Article-specific because these are dedicated lookalike/sideload hosts (manyrei.live, yandex-disk.net typosquat, offservers.ru), not a generic 'APK download' template. Rationale: Uses the exact distribution hosts and the manyrei.live/Proton_VPN.apk URL from Zimperium's zLabs RedWing IOC set (apks.csv/sites.csv); these are dedicated malicious/typosquat domains so any resolution is high-fidelity. yandex-disk.net is a lookalike of the legitimate Yandex Disk domain, used for lure hosting. Cross-checked against: • https://zimperium.com/blog/redwing-a-mobile-malware-as-a-service-operation • https://github.com/Zimperium/IOC/tree/master/2026-07-RedWing
ATT&CKT1660 T1655 T1407
Data sourcesWeb.Web
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Security researcher or MSSP analyst detonating the RedWing sample in a sandbox that egresses through the corporate proxy
  • Threat-intel enrichment tooling auto-resolving IOC domains for verdict lookups
  • A user genuinely trying to reach the legitimate Yandex Disk service and mistyping into the yandex-disk.net typosquat
  • Web crawler / URL-scanner appliance fetching flagged URLs for categorization
Suppression filter
| where RequestClientApplication !has "scanner" and RequestClientApplication !has "crawler" and DeviceProduct !in~ ("URL Filtering", "Sandbox")
Response runbook
1) Triage: identify the SourceIP/DeviceName and whether it is a mobile/BYOD asset; confirm the request was an outbound GET for an .apk (RequestURL) versus a passive scanner. 2) Contain: block all four hosts at proxy/DNS/firewall and quarantine or force-reenroll the mobile device; if the APK downloaded, pull it for analysis and revoke the user's banking/session tokens. 3) Hunt: pivot the same SourceIP to the C2 domains (krusty-crabs.sbs, redwing.top, redwingqq.top, api-sync-service.mdkd1184.workers.dev) and check for the RedWing on-device symptoms — new Accessibility/default-SMS grants and *21* call-forwarding on the handset.
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where RemoteUrl has_any ("manyrei.live/Proton_VPN.apk","manyrei.live","wmanyrei.icu","yandex-disk.net","offservers.ru")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessFileName, RemoteUrl, RemoteIP, RemotePort, InitiatingProcessCommandLine
| order by Timestamp desc
let dist = dynamic(["manyrei.live","wmanyrei.icu","yandex-disk.net","offservers.ru"]);
CommonSecurityLog
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where RequestURL has_any (dist) or DestinationHostName has_any (dist)
| project TimeGenerated, SourceIP, SourceUserName, DestinationHostName, RequestURL, RequestClientApplication, DeviceProduct
| order by TimeGenerated desc

RedWing Android banking trojan C2 beacon (krusty-crabs.sbs / redwing.top / workers.dev) AICommand & Control High
Hunts DNS/network egress to RedWing's command-and-control endpoints, including the Cloudflare Workers relay api-sync-service.mdkd1184.workers.dev used to proxy stolen SMS/OTP and VNC control traffic. Article-specific: these are the confirmed dedicated C2 hosts from Zimperium's IOC set, distinct from the Telegram rental/build channel. Rationale: Matches the four RedWing C2 domains from Zimperium's domains.csv verbatim; the workers.dev host is matched exactly (not baselined) because it is a confirmed dedicated relay, so a leading-wildcard/first-seen approach is unnecessary and any hit is malicious. Cross-checked against: • https://zimperium.com/blog/redwing-a-mobile-malware-as-a-service-operation • https://github.com/Zimperium/IOC/tree/master/2026-07-RedWing
ATT&CKT1437.001 T1521
Data sourcesNetwork_Resolution.DNS
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Sandbox/detonation of a RedWing sample egressing through corporate DNS
  • TI platform pre-resolving IOC domains for enrichment
  • Legitimate unrelated Cloudflare Workers usage (mitigated here by matching the exact api-sync-service.mdkd1184.workers.dev host, not *.workers.dev)
  • DNS sinkhole / RPZ appliance logging blocked lookups as resolutions
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm the querying asset (ClientIP/DeviceName) and whether the lookup resolved (ResultCode/answer) versus was sinkholed; treat any resolved answer from a user handset as an active infection. 2) Contain: sinkhole/block all four C2 domains, isolate or wipe-and-reenroll the device, and immediately reset the user's banking credentials and cancel any active call-forwarding on their line (RedWing sets *21* forwarding to defeat phone-based verification). 3) Hunt: back-pivot the device/IP to the delivery hosts (manyrei.live, yandex-disk.net, offservers.ru) to find the initial sideload, and sweep DNS org-wide for the same four C2 domains to scope additional victims.
let c2 = dynamic(["krusty-crabs.sbs","redwing.top","redwingqq.top","api-sync-service.mdkd1184.workers.dev"]);

| where RemoteUrl has_any (c2)
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessFileName, RemoteUrl, RemoteIP, RemotePort, InitiatingProcessCommandLine
| order by Timestamp desc
let c2 = dynamic(["krusty-crabs.sbs","redwing.top","redwingqq.top","api-sync-service.mdkd1184.workers.dev"]);
DnsEvents
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where Name has_any (c2)
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, ClientIP, Name, QueryType, ResultCode, IPAddresses = Result
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution Delivery High
User received an external email containing a URL, clicked it, and within 60 seconds the recipient's endpoint spawned a scripting interpreter or network downloader (PowerShell / cmd / mshta / curl / certutil / bitsadmin). This is the high-fidelity shape — a raw "user clicked an emailed URL" query is too noisy to alert on because every Microsoft 365 tenant generates thousands of legitimate clicks per day. The exec-correlation step suppresses the noise to roughly the rate at which a click actually drives onto-host execution, which is the actionable signal. Pair with UC_PHISH_LINK_BYPASS (Safe Links override) and UC_PHISH_LINK_NEWDOMAIN for orthogonal high-fidelity variants.
ATT&CKT1566.002 T1204.001 T1059.001
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Web Endpoint.Processes EmailEvents EmailUrlInfo UrlClickEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s.
// Far higher fidelity than "every clicked URL" — most legitimate clicks
// never spawn a non-browser child process, so the join eliminates the
// 99% of noise that makes a raw click query unactionable.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectClicks = UrlClickEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | where ActionType in ("ClickAllowed","ClickedThrough")
    | join kind=inner (
        EmailEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
        | where DeliveryAction == "Delivered"
        | where EmailDirection == "Inbound"
        | project NetworkMessageId, Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain,
                  RecipientEmailAddress, EmailTimestamp = Timestamp
      ) on NetworkMessageId
    | join kind=leftouter (
        EmailUrlInfo | project NetworkMessageId, Url, UrlDomain
      ) on NetworkMessageId, Url
    | project ClickTime = Timestamp, AccountUpn, IPAddress, Url, UrlDomain,
              Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain, RecipientEmailAddress,
              ActionType;
// Correlate to a non-browser child process spawned within 60 seconds on
// the recipient's device.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                         "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                        "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                        "bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe","curl.exe","wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectClicks on $left.AccountName == $right.AccountUpn
| where Timestamp between (ClickTime .. ClickTime + 60s)
| project ClickTime, ProcessTime = Timestamp,
          DelaySec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, ClickTime),
          DeviceName, AccountName, RecipientEmailAddress, SenderFromAddress,
          Subject, Url, UrlDomain, ActionType,
          FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by ClickTime desc
// UrlClickEvents has no clean Sentinel-native equivalent. The detection
// pivots to: Office Send→Receive proximity to SecurityEvent 4688 of a
// non-browser child process. Lower fidelity than the Defender version.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectMailUsers = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation =~ "Receive"
    | summarize Subject = any(Subject), Sender = any(Sender)
                by MailboxOwnerUPN, MessageId, EmailTime = bin(TimeGenerated, 1m);
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("\chrome.exe","\msedge.exe",
                                     "\firefox.exe","\outlook.exe","\brave.exe")
| where NewProcessName has_any ("\powershell.exe","\pwsh.exe","\cmd.exe",
                                  "\mshta.exe","\rundll32.exe","\regsvr32.exe",
                                  "\wscript.exe","\cscript.exe","\bitsadmin.exe",
                                  "\certutil.exe","\curl.exe","\wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectMailUsers on $left.Account == $right.MailboxOwnerUPN
| where TimeGenerated between (EmailTime .. EmailTime + 60s)
| project TimeGenerated, EmailTime, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName,
          NewProcessName, CommandLine, Sender, Subject
| order by TimeGenerated desc
WEB
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.

| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS click_time

         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",

Email attachment opened from external sender Delivery High
Attachment delivery + execution by recipient — most common malware initial access.
ATT&CKT1566.001 T1204.002
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Endpoint.Processes EmailAttachmentInfo DeviceProcessEvents
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let MalAttachments = EmailAttachmentInfo
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | project NetworkMessageId, RecipientEmailAddress,
              AttachmentFileName = FileName, AttachmentSHA256 = SHA256;
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("OUTLOOK.EXE","winword.exe","excel.exe","powerpnt.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                      "mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe")
| join kind=inner MalAttachments on $left.AccountUpn == $right.RecipientEmailAddress
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, AttachmentFileName, AttachmentSHA256
// Sentinel doesn't have an attachment-hash table. Best approximation:
// OfficeActivity Send/Receive activity + correlate to host process spawn.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let MailWithAttach = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation in~ ("Send","Receive")
    | where isnotempty(MessageId)
    | project EmailTime = TimeGenerated, MailboxOwnerUPN, Sender,
              Recipients, Subject, MessageId;
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName endswith "OUTLOOK.EXE"
| where NewProcessName endswith "\cmd.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\powershell.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\wscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\cscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\mshta.exe"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, NewProcessName, CommandLine,
          ParentProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Ransomware-style mass file rename / extension change Actions on Objectives Medium
Threshold detection: many files renamed in short window, often with new extension.
ATT&CKT1486
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem DeviceFileEvents
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
| where ActionType in ("FileRenamed","FileModified")
| summarize files = dcount(FileName) by DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, bin(Timestamp, 1m)
| where files > 200    // empirical: > 200 unique-file renames in 1m by one account on one host
                       //            is well above the P99 of legitimate bulk-tooling
| order by files desc

ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)
| where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
| where EventType in ("FileRenamed","FileModified")
| summarize files = dcount(TargetFileName)
            by DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName, bin(TimeGenerated, 1m)
| where files > 200    // P99 of legit bulk-tooling per-minute rename volume
| order by files desc
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count, dc(Filesystem.file_name) AS files
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem
    where Filesystem.action IN ("modified","renamed")
    by Filesystem.dest, Filesystem.user, _time span=1m
| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`
| where files > 200
| sort - files
| tstats summariesonly=false count, dc(Filesystem.file_name) AS files

| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`
| where files > 200
| sort - files
LSASS process access / dump (credential theft) Actions on Objectives High
Mimikatz, comsvcs.dll MiniDump, or any non-Windows process opening LSASS.
ATT&CKT1003.001 T1003
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes DeviceEvents
DeviceEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| where ActionType == "OpenProcessApiCall"
| where FileName =~ "lsass.exe"
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("MsSense.exe","MsMpEng.exe","csrss.exe",
                                          "svchost.exe","wininit.exe","services.exe",
                                          "lsm.exe","SearchProtocolHost.exe")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessFolderPath, AccountName
| order by Timestamp desc
// SecurityEvent EventID 4663 = object access. AccessMask 0x10 / 0x40 / 0x1010
// indicate read access to lsass.exe — credential-dump signature. Audit
// Object Access > Audit File System policy required.
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventID == 4663
| where ObjectName endswith "\lsass.exe"
| where Account !endswith "$"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, ObjectName, ProcessName,
          AccessMask, AccessReason
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Rogue Agent Flaw Could Have Let Attackers Hijack Google Dialogflow CX Chatbots

The Hacker News
2026-07-07 13 use cases 4 techniques 6 kill-chain phases detected

A critical flaw in Google's Dialogflow CX could have let an attacker with edit rights on one Code Block-enabled agent compromise other Code Block-enabled agents in the same Google Cloud project. From there, they could read live conversations, steal the data users shared, and make the bots send attacker-written messages, including requests to re-enter a password. Security firm Varonis found it
