title: Infostealer - Non-Browser Process Accessing Browser Credential Stores
id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d01
status: experimental
description: |
    Stealers (RedLine, Lumma, Vidar, Atomic) read Login Data / cookies
    SQLite databases from Chrome/Edge/Firefox profile directories. Any
    non-browser process touching these files is a high-fidelity signal.
references:
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1539/
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1555/003/
author: Clankerusecase
date: 2026/05/02
tags:
    - attack.t1539
    - attack.t1555.003
    - attack.credential-access
logsource:
    category: file_access
    product: windows
detection:
    selection_path:
        TargetFilename|contains:
            - '\Google\Chrome\User Data\'
            - '\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\'
            - '\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\'
    selection_file:
        TargetFilename|endswith:
            - '\Login Data'
            - '\Cookies'
            - '\logins.json'
            - '\cookies.sqlite'
    filter_browser:
        Image|endswith:
            - '\chrome.exe'
            - '\msedge.exe'
            - '\firefox.exe'
            - '\brave.exe'
            - '\opera.exe'
    condition: selection_path and selection_file and not filter_browser
falsepositives:
    - Backup utilities reading user profile files
    - Browser sync agents from non-stock vendors
level: high
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem
    where (Filesystem.file_path="*\Google\Chrome\User Data\*\Login Data*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Google\Chrome\User Data\*\Cookies*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\*\Login Data*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\*\logins.json*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\*\cookies.sqlite*")
      AND NOT Filesystem.process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe","brave.exe","opera.exe")
    by Filesystem.dest, Filesystem.process_name, Filesystem.file_path, Filesystem.user
| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem
    where (Filesystem.file_path="*\Google\Chrome\User Data\*\Login Data*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Google\Chrome\User Data\*\Cookies*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\*\Login Data*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\*\logins.json*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\*\cookies.sqlite*")
      AND NOT Filesystem.process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe","brave.exe","opera.exe")
    by Filesystem.dest, Filesystem.process_name, Filesystem.file_path, Filesystem.user
| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`
Ransomware-style mass file rename / extension change Actions on Objectives Medium
Threshold detection: many files renamed in short window, often with new extension.
ATT&CKT1486
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem DeviceFileEvents
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
| where ActionType in ("FileRenamed","FileModified")
| summarize files = dcount(FileName) by DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, bin(Timestamp, 1m)
| where files > 200    // empirical: > 200 unique-file renames in 1m by one account on one host
                       //            is well above the P99 of legitimate bulk-tooling
| order by files desc

ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)
| where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
| where EventType in ("FileRenamed","FileModified")
| summarize files = dcount(TargetFileName)
            by DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName, bin(TimeGenerated, 1m)
| where files > 200    // P99 of legit bulk-tooling per-minute rename volume
| order by files desc
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count, dc(Filesystem.file_name) AS files
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem
    where Filesystem.action IN ("modified","renamed")
    by Filesystem.dest, Filesystem.user, _time span=1m
| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`
| where files > 200
| sort - files
| tstats summariesonly=false count, dc(Filesystem.file_name) AS files
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem
    where Filesystem.action IN ("modified","renamed")
    by Filesystem.dest, Filesystem.user, _time span=1m
| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`
| where files > 200
| sort - files
LSASS process access / dump (credential theft) Actions on Objectives High
Mimikatz, comsvcs.dll MiniDump, or any non-Windows process opening LSASS.
ATT&CKT1003.001 T1003
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes DeviceEvents
DeviceEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| where ActionType == "OpenProcessApiCall"
| where FileName =~ "lsass.exe"
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("MsSense.exe","MsMpEng.exe","csrss.exe",
                                          "svchost.exe","wininit.exe","services.exe",
                                          "lsm.exe","SearchProtocolHost.exe")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessFolderPath, AccountName
| order by Timestamp desc
// SecurityEvent EventID 4663 = object access. AccessMask 0x10 / 0x40 / 0x1010
// indicate read access to lsass.exe — credential-dump signature. Audit
// Object Access > Audit File System policy required.
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventID == 4663
| where ObjectName endswith "\lsass.exe"
| where Account !endswith "$"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, ObjectName, ProcessName,
          AccessMask, AccessReason
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Court Filing Reveals Windows Device ID Helped FBI Trace Alleged Scattered Spider Hacker

The Hacker News
2026-07-07 16 use cases 4 techniques 5 kill-chain phases detected

U.S. prosecutors linked an alleged Scattered Spider hacker to a break-in at a luxury jewelry retailer using a persistent Windows device ID, according to a newly unsealed federal complaint. Microsoft records tied that ID first to the account the attackers used to keep access during the May 2025 intrusion, then to online accounts prosecutors say belong to 19-year-old Peter Stokes. Help-desk-driven password reset chained to MFA re-registration on privileged Entra account AIDelivery High
Hunts the Scattered Spider initial-access pattern where an IT help desk (socially engineered by phone) resets an employee password and the attacker immediately re-enrolls a new MFA method on the same account within minutes. Correlates Entra 'Reset password' with 'registered security info' for the same target user inside a 1-hour window. Rationale: Article's central thesis ('The way in was the help desk') plus CISA AA23-320A and Sygnia write-up confirm Scattered Spider resets password + re-enrolls MFA on the same account. The tight reset->MFA-registration window on an admin is the high-fidelity signal, not either event alone. Cross-checked against: • https://www.cisa.gov/news-events/cybersecurity-advisories/aa23-320a • https://www.vectra.ai/blog/the-fbi-wrote-down-the-scattered-spider-playbook-and-it-starts-with-a-phone-call
ATT&CKT1078.004 T1556.006 T1098.005
Data sourcesAuthentication.Authentication
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate help-desk password reset immediately followed by the user re-registering Authenticator after getting a new phone
  • Onboarding/offboarding automation that resets password then provisions MFA
  • Self-service password reset (SSPR) campaigns where users refresh security info
  • IT admin bulk-resetting a group of accounts during a lockout event
  • Conditional Access remediation flows forcing re-registration
Suppression filter
| where ResetActor !in~ ("sync_svc","onboarding-automation@corp.com") and MfaIP != ResetIP
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm the help-desk reset had a verified callback / ticket; check ResetIP and MfaIP geolocation and whether MfaIP is a VPN/hosting ASN (e.g. M247/Mullvad). 2) Contain: if unverified, revoke all sessions for TargetUpn, remove the newly registered MFA method, force re-enroll via verified in-person/manager channel, and disable the account if it is an IT admin. 3) Hunt: pivot on the account for ngrok/Teleport execution, new tunnel egress, sign-ins from the same anomalous IP, and any S3/cloud-storage uploads in the following hours.
let window = 1h;
let pwreset = CloudAppEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(14d)
| where ActionType in ("Reset user password.","Reset password (by admin).","Change user password.")
| extend TargetUser = tostring(ActivityObjects[0].Name)
| project ResetTime = Timestamp, TargetUser, ResetActor = AccountDisplayName, ResetIP = IPAddress;
CloudAppEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(14d)
| where ActionType in ("User registered security info","Admin registered security info","User started security info registration")
| extend TargetUser = tostring(ActivityObjects[0].Name)
| project MfaTime = Timestamp, TargetUser, MfaIP = IPAddress
| join kind=inner pwreset on TargetUser
| where MfaTime between (ResetTime .. ResetTime + window)
| project ResetTime, MfaTime, TargetUser, ResetActor, ResetIP, MfaIP, DeltaMin = datetime_diff('minute', MfaTime, ResetTime)
| order by MfaTime desc
let window = 1h;
let pwreset = AuditLogs
| where TimeGenerated > ago(14d)
| where OperationName in ("Reset password (by admin)","Reset user password","Admin reset password")
| extend TargetUpn = tostring(TargetResources[0].userPrincipalName)
| project ResetTime = TimeGenerated, TargetUpn, ResetActor = tostring(InitiatedBy.user.userPrincipalName), ResetIP = tostring(InitiatedBy.user.ipAddress);
AuditLogs
| where TimeGenerated > ago(14d)
| where OperationName in ("User registered security info","Admin registered security info","User started security info registration","User registered all required security info")
| extend TargetUpn = tostring(TargetResources[0].userPrincipalName)
| project MfaTime = TimeGenerated, TargetUpn, MfaIP = tostring(InitiatedBy.user.ipAddress)
| join kind=inner pwreset on TargetUpn
| where MfaTime between (ResetTime .. ResetTime + window)
| project ResetTime, MfaTime, TargetUpn, ResetActor, ResetIP, MfaIP, DeltaMin = datetime_diff('minute', MfaTime, ResetTime)
| order by MfaTime desc
source:azure.activeDirectory @evt.name:("Reset password (by admin)" OR "Reset user password" OR "User registered security info" OR "Admin registered security info" OR "User started security info registration")

ngrok tunnel agent execution and egress to ngrok infrastructure AICommand & Control High
Hunts execution of the ngrok agent and outbound connections to ngrok tunnel domains, the reverse-tunnel tool Scattered Spider ran on a compromised virtual server to bypass perimeter controls during the May 2025 jewelry-retailer intrusion. Covers both the process launch and the C2 channel to dashboard.ngrok.com / *.ngrok.io / *.ngrok-agent.com. Rationale: ngrok agent execution and its egress to dashboard.ngrok.com (a pre-extracted IOC) are directly named in the complaint and corroborated by CISA AA23-320A and Sygnia. Binary name + tunnel-subcommand cmdline + ngrok tunnel domains are high-fidelity and rare on servers. Cross-checked against: • https://www.cisa.gov/news-events/cybersecurity-advisories/aa23-320a • https://gbhackers.com/windows-device-track-scattered-spider-hacking-group-member/
ATT&CKT1572 T1090 T1219
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Developer using ngrok to expose a local web app for demos/webhooks
  • QA engineer tunneling a test environment
  • Legitimate SRE using ngrok for temporary remote debugging
  • Vendor/contractor with sanctioned ngrok usage in a dev subnet
Suppression filter
| where not (DeviceName has_any ("DEV-","QA-","BUILD-") and AccountName in~ ("devops","builduser"))
Response runbook
1) Triage: is the host a server or an admin workstation? ngrok on a production virtual server (as in Company F) is high-suspicion; capture the authtoken and tunnel target from the cmdline. 2) Contain: kill the ngrok process, block *.ngrok.io/*.ngrok-agent.com/*.ngrok.com at the proxy/firewall, and isolate the host if it hosts sensitive data. 3) Hunt: on the same host/account look for Teleport (tsh/teleport.exe), large outbound transfers to Amazon S3, the account's Entra password-reset/MFA-registration history, and connections to the article's VPN egress IPs.
union
(DeviceProcessEvents
 | where Timestamp > ago(30d)
 | where FileName =~ "ngrok.exe" or ProcessCommandLine has_any ("ngrok tcp","ngrok http","ngrok start","--authtoken")
 | where AccountName !endswith "$"
 | project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, Signal="process", Detail=ProcessCommandLine, FileName),
(DeviceNetworkEvents
 | where Timestamp > ago(30d)
 | where RemoteUrl has_any ("ngrok.com","ngrok.io","ngrok-agent.com")
 | project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName=InitiatingProcessAccountName, Signal="network", Detail=RemoteUrl, FileName=InitiatingProcessFileName)
| order by Timestamp desc
union
(ImProcessCreate
 | where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
 | where ActingProcessName has "ngrok.exe" or ActingProcessCommandLine has_any ("ngrok tcp","ngrok http","ngrok start","--authtoken")
 | project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, Signal="process", Detail=ActingProcessCommandLine),
(ImDnsActivity
 | where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
 | where DnsQuery has_any ("ngrok.com","ngrok.io","ngrok-agent.com")
 | project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername=SrcUsername, Signal="dns", Detail=DnsQuery)
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Teleport (tsh/teleport.exe) remote-access tool execution and egress to teleport.sh AIInstallation Medium
Hunts the second tunneling tool named in the complaint — Teleport.sh — via execution of tsh/teleport/tbot binaries or connections to teleport.sh, which Scattered Spider used alongside ngrok to move ~99.5 MB of tooling in and exfiltrate data out of the retailer's network. Rationale: Teleport.sh is explicitly named in the complaint (corroborated by Sygnia/CISA reporting) as the second tunnel used to stage tooling and exfiltrate 77 GB. tsh/teleport/tbot binaries and teleport.sh egress are article-specific; kept as hunting because Teleport is legitimate infra software. Cross-checked against: • https://www.cisa.gov/news-events/cybersecurity-advisories/aa23-320a • https://gbhackers.com/windows-device-track-scattered-spider-hacking-group-member/
ATT&CKT1219 T1572
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Organization legitimately runs Gravitational/Teleport for zero-trust SSH/Kubernetes access
  • Platform engineers using tsh to reach bastion hosts
  • CI/CD pipelines using tbot for machine identity
  • Contractor with sanctioned Teleport cluster access
Suppression filter
| where not (Detail has_any ("corp-teleport.internal","teleport.corp.local"))
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm whether your org operates a sanctioned Teleport cluster; if not, any tsh/teleport execution is anomalous. Check the destination proxy in the cmdline (own cluster vs teleport.sh SaaS). 2) Contain: kill the process, block teleport.sh egress, and isolate the host if it holds sensitive data. 3) Hunt: correlate with ngrok on the same host, the account's help-desk reset history, and outbound bulk transfers to Amazon S3.
union
(DeviceProcessEvents
 | where Timestamp > ago(30d)
 | where FileName in~ ("tsh.exe","teleport.exe","tbot.exe") or ProcessCommandLine has_any ("tsh login","tsh scp","tsh ssh","teleport.sh")
 | where AccountName !endswith "$"
 | project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, Signal="process", Detail=ProcessCommandLine, FileName),
(DeviceNetworkEvents
 | where Timestamp > ago(30d)
 | where RemoteUrl has "teleport.sh"
 | project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName=InitiatingProcessAccountName, Signal="network", Detail=RemoteUrl, FileName=InitiatingProcessFileName)
| order by Timestamp desc
union
(ImProcessCreate
 | where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
 | where ActingProcessName has_any ("tsh.exe","teleport.exe","tbot.exe") or ActingProcessCommandLine has_any ("tsh login","tsh scp","teleport.sh")
 | project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, Signal="process", Detail=ActingProcessCommandLine),
(ImDnsActivity
 | where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
 | where DnsQuery has "teleport.sh"
 | project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername=SrcUsername, Signal="dns", Detail=DnsQuery)
| order by TimeGenerated desc

  selection_cmd:

Bulk data staging to Amazon S3 by a tunneling/transfer tool AIActions on Objectives Medium
Hunts data exfiltration to Amazon S3 initiated by the same tunneling/transfer tooling (ngrok, Teleport tsh, rclone, aws-cli, curl) that Scattered Spider used to move 77 GB out of the retailer's environment. Focuses on non-browser processes reaching *.amazonaws.com from an interactive user context. Rationale: The complaint and Sygnia reporting state exfiltration used Teleport.sh + Amazon S3 for 77 GB. Pairing the named tunneling/transfer binaries with an amazonaws.com destination isolates attacker exfil from normal browser-based S3 usage; kept hunting due to legitimate aws-cli/rclone S3 traffic. Cross-checked against: • https://gbhackers.com/windows-device-track-scattered-spider-hacking-group-member/ • https://www.cisa.gov/news-events/cybersecurity-advisories/aa23-320a
ATT&CKT1567.002 T1048
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Backup/DR jobs using rclone or aws-cli to sync to S3
  • Developers uploading build artifacts to an S3 bucket via aws-cli
  • Legitimate curl-based deployment scripts hitting S3-hosted assets
  • Log-shipping agents forwarding to an S3 sink
Suppression filter
| where not (InitiatingProcessAccountName in~ ("svc-backup","veeam") or DeviceName has "BACKUP-")
Response runbook
1) Triage: identify the destination bucket/endpoint and whether it belongs to your org's AWS accounts; attacker exfil goes to an EXTERNAL/attacker-controlled bucket. Estimate volume moved. 2) Contain: kill the transfer process, block the S3 endpoint if external, revoke the user's sessions, and preserve the host for forensics. 3) Hunt: tie back to ngrok/Teleport execution, the help-desk reset chain, and connections to the article's VPN egress IPs; scope which sensitive data stores the account touched.
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where RemoteUrl endswith "amazonaws.com"
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("ngrok.exe","tsh.exe","teleport.exe","tbot.exe","rclone.exe","aws.exe","curl.exe")
| where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
| summarize ConnCount=count(), FirstSeen=min(Timestamp), LastSeen=max(Timestamp), Endpoints=make_set(RemoteUrl, 20) by DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName
| where ConnCount >= 5
| order by ConnCount desc
ImNetworkSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where DstHostname endswith "amazonaws.com" or Url has "amazonaws.com"
| where SrcUsername != "" and SrcUsername !endswith "$"
| summarize ConnCount=count(), TotalBytes=sum(NetworkBytes), FirstSeen=min(TimeGenerated), LastSeen=max(TimeGenerated) by SrcHostname, SrcUsername, DstHostname
| where TotalBytes > 1073741824 or ConnCount >= 20
| order by TotalBytes desc

Egress to Scattered Spider VPN/proxy IP set from the jewelry-retailer complaint AICommand & Control Low
Watchlist hunt for outbound connections to the 12 attacker source IPs (largely M247/Mullvad-style VPN egress) listed in the federal complaint, several of which were the proxy the actor used to reach the retailer and open the ngrok account. Low-confidence/single-source IOC feed — treat hits as an enrichment pivot, not a standalone alert. Rationale: These 12 IPs are the pre-extracted IOCs from the complaint (the proxy that opened the ngrok account and reached the retailer). Confidence deliberately Low: they are single-source (court filing) and mostly shared VPN egress (M247/Mullvad), so hits need corroboration with the ngrok/Teleport/S3 behaviors above before actioning. Cross-checked against: • https://gbhackers.com/windows-device-track-scattered-spider-hacking-group-member/
ATT&CKT1090.003 T1572
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic
Expected false positives · estimated rate: high — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Employees or contractors legitimately using Mullvad/M247 VPN egress
  • Security researchers/pentesters routing through the same shared VPN pool
  • IP re-allocation to a benign VPN tenant after the incident
  • Threat-intel scanning or sandbox detonation traffic from your own tooling
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm the internal host/account and whether the connection is inbound (someone reaching your exposed service via this proxy) or outbound; check if the peer process is ngrok/Teleport. 2) Contain: block the IP at perimeter, and if tied to an admin account revoke sessions and reset credentials via a verified channel. 3) Hunt: pivot to the help-desk reset/MFA-registration chain, ngrok/Teleport execution, and S3 uploads on the same host/account within the surrounding window; only escalate the IP hit if one of those corroborates.

title: Infostealer - Non-Browser Process Accessing Browser Credential Stores
id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d01
status: experimental
description: |
    Stealers (RedLine, Lumma, Vidar, Atomic) read Login Data / cookies
    SQLite databases from Chrome/Edge/Firefox profile directories. Any
    non-browser process touching these files is a high-fidelity signal.
references:

author: Clankerusecase
date: 2026/05/02

logsource:

detection:

            - '\Google\Chrome\User Data\'
            - '\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\'

    selection_file:

            - '\Login Data'

level: high

Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem
    where (Filesystem.file_path="*\Google\Chrome\User Data\*\Login Data*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Google\Chrome\User Data\*\Cookies*"

        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\*\cookies.sqlite*")

    by Filesystem.dest, Filesystem.process_name, Filesystem.file_path, Filesystem.user
| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem
    where (Filesystem.file_path="*\Google\Chrome\User Data\*\Login Data*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Google\Chrome\User Data\*\Cookies*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\*\Login Data*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\*\logins.json*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\*\cookies.sqlite*")
      AND NOT Filesystem.process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe","brave.exe","opera.exe")
    by Filesystem.dest, Filesystem.process_name, Filesystem.file_path, Filesystem.user
| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`
Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution Delivery High
User received an external email containing a URL, clicked it, and within 60 seconds the recipient's endpoint spawned a scripting interpreter or network downloader (PowerShell / cmd / mshta / curl / certutil / bitsadmin). This is the high-fidelity shape — a raw "user clicked an emailed URL" query is too noisy to alert on because every Microsoft 365 tenant generates thousands of legitimate clicks per day. The exec-correlation step suppresses the noise to roughly the rate at which a click actually drives onto-host execution, which is the actionable signal. Pair with UC_PHISH_LINK_BYPASS (Safe Links override) and UC_PHISH_LINK_NEWDOMAIN for orthogonal high-fidelity variants.
ATT&CKT1566.002 T1204.001 T1059.001
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Web Endpoint.Processes EmailEvents EmailUrlInfo UrlClickEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s.
// Far higher fidelity than "every clicked URL" — most legitimate clicks
// never spawn a non-browser child process, so the join eliminates the
// 99% of noise that makes a raw click query unactionable.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectClicks = UrlClickEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | where ActionType in ("ClickAllowed","ClickedThrough")
    | join kind=inner (
        EmailEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
        | where DeliveryAction == "Delivered"
        | where EmailDirection == "Inbound"
        | project NetworkMessageId, Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain,
                  RecipientEmailAddress, EmailTimestamp = Timestamp
      ) on NetworkMessageId
    | join kind=leftouter (
        EmailUrlInfo | project NetworkMessageId, Url, UrlDomain
      ) on NetworkMessageId, Url
    | project ClickTime = Timestamp, AccountUpn, IPAddress, Url, UrlDomain,
              Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain, RecipientEmailAddress,
              ActionType;
// Correlate to a non-browser child process spawned within 60 seconds on
// the recipient's device.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                         "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                        "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                        "bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe","curl.exe","wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectClicks on $left.AccountName == $right.AccountUpn
| where Timestamp between (ClickTime .. ClickTime + 60s)
| project ClickTime, ProcessTime = Timestamp,
          DelaySec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, ClickTime),
          DeviceName, AccountName, RecipientEmailAddress, SenderFromAddress,
          Subject, Url, UrlDomain, ActionType,
          FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by ClickTime desc
// UrlClickEvents has no clean Sentinel-native equivalent. The detection
// pivots to: Office Send→Receive proximity to SecurityEvent 4688 of a
// non-browser child process. Lower fidelity than the Defender version.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectMailUsers = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation =~ "Receive"
    | summarize Subject = any(Subject), Sender = any(Sender)
                by MailboxOwnerUPN, MessageId, EmailTime = bin(TimeGenerated, 1m);
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("\chrome.exe","\msedge.exe",
                                     "\firefox.exe","\outlook.exe","\brave.exe")
| where NewProcessName has_any ("\powershell.exe","\pwsh.exe","\cmd.exe",
                                  "\mshta.exe","\rundll32.exe","\regsvr32.exe",
                                  "\wscript.exe","\cscript.exe","\bitsadmin.exe",
                                  "\certutil.exe","\curl.exe","\wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectMailUsers on $left.Account == $right.MailboxOwnerUPN
| where TimeGenerated between (EmailTime .. EmailTime + 60s)
| project TimeGenerated, EmailTime, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName,
          NewProcessName, CommandLine, Sender, Subject
| order by TimeGenerated desc
WEB
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"
    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| rename user AS recipient, dest AS clicked_domain, url AS clicked_url
| join type=inner recipient
    [| tstats `summariesonly` count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"
         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"
     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",
                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
     | rename dest AS src]
| eval delta_sec = exec_time - click_time
| where delta_sec >= 0 AND delta_sec <= 60
| table click_time, exec_time, delta_sec, recipient, src, src_user, subject,
        clicked_domain, clicked_url, exec_proc, exec_cmd
| sort - click_time
``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats summariesonly=false earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"
    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| rename user AS recipient, dest AS clicked_domain, url AS clicked_url

    [| tstats summariesonly=false count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"
         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"
     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats summariesonly=false earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",
                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
     | rename dest AS src]
| eval delta_sec = exec_time - click_time
| where delta_sec >= 0 AND delta_sec <= 60

Email attachment opened from external sender Delivery High
Attachment delivery + execution by recipient — most common malware initial access.
ATT&CKT1566.001 T1204.002
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Endpoint.Processes EmailAttachmentInfo DeviceProcessEvents
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let MalAttachments = EmailAttachmentInfo
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | project NetworkMessageId, RecipientEmailAddress,
              AttachmentFileName = FileName, AttachmentSHA256 = SHA256;
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("OUTLOOK.EXE","winword.exe","excel.exe","powerpnt.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                      "mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe")
| join kind=inner MalAttachments on $left.AccountUpn == $right.RecipientEmailAddress
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, AttachmentFileName, AttachmentSHA256
// Sentinel doesn't have an attachment-hash table. Best approximation:
// OfficeActivity Send/Receive activity + correlate to host process spawn.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let MailWithAttach = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation in~ ("Send","Receive")
    | where isnotempty(MessageId)
    | project EmailTime = TimeGenerated, MailboxOwnerUPN, Sender,
              Recipients, Subject, MessageId;
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName endswith "OUTLOOK.EXE"
| where NewProcessName endswith "\cmd.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\powershell.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\wscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\cscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\mshta.exe"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, NewProcessName, CommandLine,
          ParentProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count
    from datamodel=Email.All_Email
    where All_Email.file_name!="-"
    by All_Email.src_user, All_Email.recipient, All_Email.file_name, All_Email.subject
| rename All_Email.recipient as user
| join type=inner user
    [| tstats `summariesonly` count
        from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
        where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("OUTLOOK.EXE","winword.exe","excel.exe","powerpnt.exe")
          AND Processes.process_name IN ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe","mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe")
        by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.parent_process_name, Processes.process_name, Processes.process
     | rename Processes.user as user]
| tstats summariesonly=false count
    from datamodel=Email.All_Email
    where All_Email.file_name!="-"
    by All_Email.src_user, All_Email.recipient, All_Email.file_name, All_Email.subject
| rename All_Email.recipient as user
| join type=inner user
    [| tstats summariesonly=false count
        from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
        where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("OUTLOOK.EXE","winword.exe","excel.exe","powerpnt.exe")
          AND Processes.process_name IN ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe","mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe")
        by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.parent_process_name, Processes.process_name, Processes.process
     | rename Processes.user as user]
Office app spawning script/LOLBin child process Exploitation High
Classic macro/exploit pattern — Office app launching cmd/powershell/wmic/regsvr32.
ATT&CKT1059.001 T1059.005 T1218
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes DeviceProcessEvents
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("winword.exe","excel.exe","powerpnt.exe","outlook.exe","onenote.exe","mspub.exe","visio.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe","mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wmic.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where Account !endswith "$"
| where ParentProcessName endswith "\winword.exe"
   or ParentProcessName endswith "\excel.exe"
   or ParentProcessName endswith "\powerpnt.exe"
   or ParentProcessName endswith "\outlook.exe"
   or ParentProcessName endswith "\onenote.exe"
   or ParentProcessName endswith "\mspub.exe"
   or ParentProcessName endswith "\visio.exe"
| where NewProcessName endswith "\cmd.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\powershell.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\pwsh.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\wscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\cscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\mshta.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\rundll32.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\regsvr32.exe"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName,
          NewProcessName, CommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc

title: Office Application Spawning Script Host
id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d07
status: experimental
description: |
    Word/Excel/Outlook/OneNote spawning powershell, cmd, wscript,
    cscript, mshta, rundll32, regsvr32 — classic macro / embedded-
    object payload signature.
references:
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1059/
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1566/001/
author: Clankerusecase
date: 2026/05/02
tags:
    - attack.t1059
    - attack.t1566.001
    - attack.execution
logsource:
    category: process_creation
    product: windows
detection:
    selection_parent:
        ParentImage|endswith:
            - '\winword.exe'
            - '\excel.exe'
            - '\powerpnt.exe'
            - '\outlook.exe'
            - '\onenote.exe'
            - '\mspub.exe'
            - '\visio.exe'
    selection_child:
        Image|endswith:
            - '\cmd.exe'
            - '\powershell.exe'
            - '\pwsh.exe'
            - '\wscript.exe'
            - '\cscript.exe'
            - '\mshta.exe'
            - '\rundll32.exe'
            - '\regsvr32.exe'
    condition: selection_parent and selection_child
falsepositives:
    - Legitimate automation macros in trusted internal documents
level: high
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
    where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("winword.exe","excel.exe","powerpnt.exe","outlook.exe","onenote.exe","mspub.exe","visio.exe")
      AND Processes.process_name IN ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe","mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wmic.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe")
    by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.parent_process_name, Processes.process_name, Processes.process
| `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
| `security_content_ctime(firstTime)` | `security_content_ctime(lastTime)`
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
    where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("winword.exe","excel.exe","powerpnt.exe","outlook.exe","onenote.exe","mspub.exe","visio.exe")
      AND Processes.process_name IN ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe","mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wmic.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe")
    by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.parent_process_name, Processes.process_name, Processes.process
| `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
| `security_content_ctime(firstTime)` | `security_content_ctime(lastTime)`
Microsoft Teams external-tenant chat from unverified IT-helpdesk impersonator Delivery High
External Teams chat where displayName contains 'helpdesk' or 'IT support' — common 2024+ vishing pattern (Storm-1811, Black Basta, UNC6692). No CIM data model maps to Teams chats; uses raw O365 audit logs.
ATT&CKT1566.004 T1566
Data sourcesCloudAppEvents
CloudAppEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where Application == "Microsoft Teams"
| where ActionType == "MessageSent"
| where RawEventData has "ExternalParticipants"
| extend SenderDisplayName = tostring(parse_json(RawEventData).SenderDisplayName)
| where SenderDisplayName matches regex @"(?i)(help.?desk|it.?support|service.?desk|tech.?support|admin)"
| project Timestamp, AccountDisplayName, IPAddress, ActivityType, SenderDisplayName, RawEventData
// External Teams chat — Teams audit lives in OfficeActivity.
OfficeActivity
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where OfficeWorkload == "MicrosoftTeams"
| where Operation in~ ("MessageSent","ChatCreated","TeamsImpersonationDetected")
| where isnotempty(UserId)
| where Subject has_any ("IT","helpdesk","support","password","verify")
   or Recipients has_any ("IT","helpdesk")
| project TimeGenerated, UserId, Operation, Subject, Recipients,
          ClientIP, UserAgent
| order by TimeGenerated desc
CLOUD
`o365_management_activity`
  Workload=MicrosoftTeams Operation=MessageSent
  ExternalParticipants=*
| where match(SenderDisplayName, "(?i)(help.?desk|it.?support|service.?desk|tech.?support|admin)")
| stats count, earliest(_time) as firstTime, latest(_time) as lastTime
    by SenderUpn, SenderDisplayName, RecipientUpn, ChatId
RMM tool installed by non-IT user — remote-access utility for hands-on-keyboard Installation High
ConnectWise / AnyDesk / TeamViewer / ScreenConnect / Atera installed outside IT change windows = common tradecraft for ransomware affiliates and IT-helpdesk impersonators.
ATT&CKT1219
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes DeviceProcessEvents
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| where FileName in~ ("AnyDesk.exe","TeamViewer.exe","TeamViewer_Service.exe",
        "ScreenConnect.ClientService.exe","ConnectWiseControl.ClientService.exe",
        "atera_agent.exe","SplashtopStreamer.exe","RustDesk.exe","NinjaOne.exe")
   or FileName matches regex @"(?i)kaseya.*\.exe"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where Account !endswith "$"
| where NewProcessName endswith "\AnyDesk.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\TeamViewer.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\TeamViewer_Service.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\ScreenConnect.ClientService.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\ConnectWiseControl.ClientService.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\atera_agent.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\SplashtopStreamer.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\RustDesk.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\NinjaOne.exe"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, NewProcessName,
          CommandLine, ParentProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc

title: Remote-Management (RMM) Tool Execution
id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d0c
status: experimental
description: |
    AnyDesk / TeamViewer / ScreenConnect / Atera / Splashtop /
    RustDesk — RMM tools attackers commonly install for hands-on-
    keyboard access. Filter against the IT estate's known tool.
references:
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1219/
author: Clankerusecase
date: 2026/05/02
tags:
    - attack.t1219
    - attack.command-and-control
logsource:
    category: process_creation
    product: windows
detection:
    selection:
        Image|endswith:
            - '\AnyDesk.exe'
            - '\TeamViewer.exe'
            - '\TeamViewer_Service.exe'
            - '\ScreenConnect.ClientService.exe'
            - '\ConnectWiseControl.ClientService.exe'
            - '\atera_agent.exe'
            - '\SplashtopStreamer.exe'
            - '\RustDesk.exe'
            - '\NinjaOne.exe'
    condition: selection
falsepositives:
    - IT-approved RMM in use across the estate. Maintain a known-IT-
      tool exclusion list per environment.
level: high
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
    where Processes.process_name IN ("AnyDesk.exe","TeamViewer.exe","TeamViewer_Service.exe",
        "ScreenConnect.ClientService.exe","ConnectWiseControl.ClientService.exe",
        "atera_agent.exe","SplashtopStreamer.exe","RustDesk.exe","NinjaOne.exe","kaseya*.exe")
    by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.process_name, Processes.process, Processes.parent_process_name
| `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
    where Processes.process_name IN ("AnyDesk.exe","TeamViewer.exe","TeamViewer_Service.exe",
        "ScreenConnect.ClientService.exe","ConnectWiseControl.ClientService.exe",
        "atera_agent.exe","SplashtopStreamer.exe","RustDesk.exe","NinjaOne.exe","kaseya*.exe")
    by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.process_name, Processes.process, Processes.parent_process_name
| `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
Ransomware-style mass file rename / extension change Actions on Objectives Medium
Threshold detection: many files renamed in short window, often with new extension.
ATT&CKT1486
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem DeviceFileEvents
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
| where ActionType in ("FileRenamed","FileModified")
| summarize files = dcount(FileName) by DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, bin(Timestamp, 1m)
| where files > 200    // empirical: > 200 unique-file renames in 1m by one account on one host
                       //            is well above the P99 of legitimate bulk-tooling
| order by files desc

ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)
| where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
| where EventType in ("FileRenamed","FileModified")
| summarize files = dcount(TargetFileName)
            by DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName, bin(TimeGenerated, 1m)
| where files > 200    // P99 of legit bulk-tooling per-minute rename volume
| order by files desc
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count, dc(Filesystem.file_name) AS files
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem
    where Filesystem.action IN ("modified","renamed")
    by Filesystem.dest, Filesystem.user, _time span=1m
| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`
| where files > 200
| sort - files
| tstats summariesonly=false count, dc(Filesystem.file_name) AS files
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem
    where Filesystem.action IN ("modified","renamed")
    by Filesystem.dest, Filesystem.user, _time span=1m
| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`
| where files > 200
| sort - files
LSASS process access / dump (credential theft) Actions on Objectives High
Mimikatz, comsvcs.dll MiniDump, or any non-Windows process opening LSASS.
ATT&CKT1003.001 T1003
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes DeviceEvents
DeviceEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| where ActionType == "OpenProcessApiCall"
| where FileName =~ "lsass.exe"
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("MsSense.exe","MsMpEng.exe","csrss.exe",
                                          "svchost.exe","wininit.exe","services.exe",
                                          "lsm.exe","SearchProtocolHost.exe")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessFolderPath, AccountName
| order by Timestamp desc
// SecurityEvent EventID 4663 = object access. AccessMask 0x10 / 0x40 / 0x1010
// indicate read access to lsass.exe — credential-dump signature. Audit
// Object Access > Audit File System policy required.
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventID == 4663
| where ObjectName endswith "\lsass.exe"
| where Account !endswith "$"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, ObjectName, ProcessName,
          AccessMask, AccessReason
| order by TimeGenerated desc

title: LSASS Process Access Outside Microsoft-Signed Tooling
id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d04
status: experimental
description: |
    Anything opening lsass.exe with read-memory access that isn't a
    Microsoft signed component (Defender, csrss, etc.) is suspect.
    Mimikatz / Pypykatz / nanodump signature.
references:
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1003/001/
author: Clankerusecase
date: 2026/05/02
tags:
    - attack.t1003.001
    - attack.credential-access
logsource:
    category: process_access
    product: windows
detection:
    selection:
        TargetImage|endswith: '\lsass.exe'
    filter_known_good:
        SourceImage|endswith:
            - '\MsSense.exe'
            - '\MsMpEng.exe'
            - '\csrss.exe'
            - '\svchost.exe'
            - '\wininit.exe'
            - '\services.exe'
            - '\lsm.exe'
            - '\SearchProtocolHost.exe'
    condition: selection and not filter_known_good
falsepositives:
    - Third-party EDR / forensic tools — extend the filter list
level: high
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
    where (Processes.process="*lsass*" OR Processes.process="*sekurlsa*"
        OR Processes.process="*MiniDump*" OR Processes.process="*comsvcs.dll*MiniDump*"
        OR Processes.process="*procdump*lsass*")
       OR (Processes.process_name="rundll32.exe" AND Processes.process="*comsvcs*MiniDump*")
    by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.process_name, Processes.process, Processes.parent_process_name
| `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
    where (Processes.process="*lsass*" OR Processes.process="*sekurlsa*"
        OR Processes.process="*MiniDump*" OR Processes.process="*comsvcs.dll*MiniDump*"
        OR Processes.process="*procdump*lsass*")
       OR (Processes.process_name="rundll32.exe" AND Processes.process="*comsvcs*MiniDump*")
    by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.process_name, Processes.process, Processes.parent_process_name
| `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`

title: PsExec / SMB Lateral Movement Tooling Execution
id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d03
status: experimental
description: |
    PsExec, paexec, smbexec, csexec, remcom — admin-grade tooling that
    pivots over SMB. Pair with `wmic /node:` for the full cluster.
references:
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1021/002/
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1569/002/
author: Clankerusecase
date: 2026/05/02
tags:
    - attack.t1021.002
    - attack.t1569.002
    - attack.lateral-movement
    - attack.execution
logsource:
    category: process_creation
    product: windows
detection:
    selection_psexec:
        Image|endswith:
            - '\psexec.exe'
            - '\psexec64.exe'
            - '\psexesvc.exe'
            - '\paexec.exe'
            - '\csexec.exe'
            - '\remcom.exe'
            - '\smbexec.py'
    selection_wmic_remote:
        Image|endswith:
            - '\wmic.exe'
        CommandLine|contains:
            - '/node:'
    condition: selection_psexec or selection_wmic_remote
falsepositives:
    - Sysadmins running approved remote-management tooling — wrap with
      a known-admin-host watchlist
level: high
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
    where Processes.process_name IN ("psexec.exe","psexesvc.exe","paexec.exe","smbexec.py")
       OR (Processes.process_name="wmic.exe" AND Processes.process="*/node:*")
    by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.process_name, Processes.process, Processes.parent_process_name
| `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
    where Processes.process_name IN ("psexec.exe","psexesvc.exe","paexec.exe","smbexec.py")
       OR (Processes.process_name="wmic.exe" AND Processes.process="*/node:*")
    by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.process_name, Processes.process, Processes.parent_process_name
| `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
Network connections to article IPs / domains Command & Control High

title: Outbound Connection to Article-Named IP / Domain
id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d0f
status: experimental
description: |
    Replace `__IP_LIST__` / `__DOMAIN_LIST__` placeholders with
    article-specific destinations. For dynamic IOC management, use a
    watchlist or external feed.
references:
    - https://attack.mitre.org/tactics/TA0011/
author: Clankerusecase
date: 2026/05/02
tags:
    - attack.command-and-control
logsource:
    category: network_connection
    product: windows
detection:
    selection_ip:
        DestinationIp:
            - '__IP_PLACEHOLDER_1__'
            - '__IP_PLACEHOLDER_2__'
    selection_domain:
        DestinationHostname:
            - '__DOMAIN_PLACEHOLDER_1__'
            - '__DOMAIN_PLACEHOLDER_2__'
    condition: selection_ip or selection_domain
falsepositives:
    - None on a true-positive IOC match
level: critical
NETWORK
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Network_Traffic.All_Traffic
    where All_Traffic.dest IN ("146.70.134.82", "79.127.222.213", "146.70.126.237", "193.32.127.231", "146.70.126.215", "138.199.6.242", "46.19.136.247", "138.199.6.216", "193.32.248.138", "146.70.126.183", "23.234.88.97", "146.70.134.23")
    by All_Traffic.src, All_Traffic.dest, All_Traffic.dest_port
| `drop_dm_object_name(All_Traffic)`
| append
    [| tstats `summariesonly` count from datamodel=Web
        where Web.dest IN ("dashboard.ngrok.com")
        by Web.src, Web.dest, Web.url, Web.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`]

EGroupware CVE-2026-27823 arbitrary file read via importexport download path traversal AIExploitation High
Hunts inbound HTTP requests to the EGroupware importexport export handler carrying a traversal-laden _filename parameter. This is the arbitrary-file-read primitive attackers use to exfiltrate a valid header.inc.php before overwriting it for RCE — article-specific because it pins the exact vulnerable menuaction and parameter. Rationale: Anchors on the exact vulnerable menuaction 'importexport.importexport_export_ui.download' plus a path-traversal _filename token straight from the advisory's PoC URL — the pair is not something benign EGroupware traffic produces. Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-h9qx-v5xp-ph8p • https://www.cvedetails.com/vulnerability-list/vendor_id-2373/Egroupware.html
ATT&CKT1190 T1083
Data sourcesWeb.Web
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Vulnerability scanners (Nessus/Qualys/Nuclei) probing EGroupware with traversal templates
  • Internal pentest or red-team validation of CVE-2026-27823
  • Security researcher testing after patch to confirm remediation
  • WAF in monitor-mode logging blocked-then-passed requests
Suppression filter
| where HttpStatusCode == 200
Response runbook
1) TRIAGE: Confirm the HTTP status — a 200 with a non-trivial response body means the file read succeeded; extract SrcIpAddr and check whether _filename resolved to header.inc.php or another sensitive file. 2) CONTAIN: Block the source IP at the WAF/edge and confirm EGroupware is patched (>= 26.2.20260224 / >= 23.1.20260224); disable user self-registration if enabled. 3) HUNT: Pivot on the same SrcIpAddr for subsequent POST uploads to the SmallPart media recorder and for any modification of header.inc.php on the host.
ImWebSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where Url has "menuaction=importexport.importexport_export_ui.download"
| where Url has_any ("_filename=../", "_filename=..%2f", "%2e%2e%2f", "..%5c", "header.inc.php")
| project TimeGenerated, SrcIpAddr, DstHostname, HttpMethod, HttpStatusCode, Url
| order by TimeGenerated desc
title: EGroupware importexport Arbitrary File Read via Path Traversal (CVE-2026-27823)
id: 6b2f9c1a-4d7e-4b21-9a3c-1e5f8c0a7d42
description: Detects requests to the EGroupware importexport_export_ui.download handler carrying a traversal _filename parameter, the arbitrary file read primitive of CVE-2026-27823.
references:
  - https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-h9qx-v5xp-ph8p
author: SOC Detection Engineering
date: 2026/07/07
tags:
  - attack.t1190
  - attack.t1083
logsource:
  category: webserver
detection:
  selection:
    c-uri|contains: 'menuaction=importexport.importexport_export_ui.download'
  traversal:
    c-uri|contains:
      - '_filename=../'
      - '_filename=..%2f'
      - '%2e%2e%2f'
      - '..%5c'
  condition: selection and traversal
level: high
WEB
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Web where Web.url="*menuaction=importexport.importexport_export_ui.download*" AND (Web.url="*_filename=../*" OR Web.url="*_filename=..%2f*" OR Web.url="*%2e%2e%2f*" OR Web.url="*header.inc.php*") by Web.src Web.dest Web.http_method Web.status Web.url | `drop_dm_object_name(Web)` | convert ctime(firstTime) ctime(lastTime)
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Web where Web.url="*menuaction=importexport.importexport_export_ui.download*" AND (Web.url="*_filename=../*" OR Web.url="*_filename=..%2f*" OR Web.url="*%2e%2e%2f*" OR Web.url="*header.inc.php*") by Web.src Web.dest Web.http_method Web.status Web.url | `drop_dm_object_name(Web)` | convert ctime(firstTime) ctime(lastTime)
EGroupware header.inc.php overwritten by web process (CVE-2026-27823 RCE persistence) AIInstallation High
Detects the web/PHP runtime writing or modifying header.inc.php — EGroupware's core bootstrap config, which is normally only written during setup. In CVE-2026-27823 the auth-bypass file-write primitive overwrites this file with attacker PHP to achieve RCE on restart/OPcache expiry. Rationale: header.inc.php is EGroupware's bootstrap config; a write to it by php/php-fpm/apache at runtime (not during setup) is the exact RCE persistence artifact named in the advisory. Filename + web-process parent make it very high-fidelity. Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-h9qx-v5xp-ph8p
ATT&CKT1505.003 T1190
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate EGroupware setup/reconfiguration wizard writing header.inc.php
  • Admin editing config via the setup UI after an upgrade
  • Automated deployment/config-management (Ansible/Puppet) templating header.inc.php — but that runs as a deploy user, not php-fpm
  • Package upgrade regenerating the config file
Suppression filter
| where not (InitiatingProcessCommandLine has_any ("setup","cli.php","doctrine") )
Response runbook
1) TRIAGE: Diff the new header.inc.php against a known-good copy; look for injected PHP (system/exec/passthru, base64 blobs, added functions) beyond the expected config array. 2) CONTAIN: Restore header.inc.php from backup, kill the php-fpm/apache workers, and take the host off the network if injected code is present. 3) HUNT: Search DeviceProcessEvents for php-fpm/apache spawning shells or network tools, and review web logs for the preceding SmallPart ajax_upload POST and importexport file-read that seeded the attack.

| where FileName =~ "header.inc.php"
| where ActionType in ("FileCreated","FileModified","FileRenamed")
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("php","php-fpm","php-fpm8","apache2","httpd","nginx") or InitiatingProcessFolderPath has_any ("/var/www","/usr/share/egroupware")

| order by Timestamp desc

| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, TargetFilePath, TargetFileName, EventType, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine, ActorUsername
| order by TimeGenerated desc

EGroupware web runtime (php-fpm/apache) spawning a shell or network tool — CVE-2026-27823 RCE execution AIActions on Objectives Medium
Hunts the PHP/web server process spawning interactive shells or download utilities, the observable execution stage once CVE-2026-27823's poisoned header.inc.php runs. Article-specific because EGroupware executes as www-data under php-fpm/apache, so shell children of that process are anomalous. Rationale: The advisory states EGroupware runs as www-data under the web server and achieves RCE via header.inc.php; a php-fpm/apache parent spawning a shell or curl/wget is the direct execution signature of that RCE, keyed on the runtime's own process names. Non-virtualization process accessing /dev/kvm on KVM host (Januscape CVE-2026-53359 LPE precursor) AIExploitation Medium
Hunts local processes that open or reference /dev/kvm on a hypervisor host while NOT being part of the legitimate virtualization stack (qemu/libvirt/firecracker/etc.). On RHEL and other distros where /dev/kvm is world-writable, an unprivileged local user can drive the CVE-2026-53359 shadow-MMU use-after-free through this device to gain root — so an unexpected opener is the earliest host-side signal of exploitation. Rationale: Uses the article's concrete device path (/dev/kvm) and the explicit RHEL world-writable-device LPE condition; the virtualization-stack allowlist keeps qemu/libvirt/firecracker noise out so a residual hit is an unexpected opener. Cross-checked TheHackerNews and the oss-security disclosure which name kvm_mmu_get_child_sp() and confirm the unprivileged /dev/kvm path. Cross-checked against: • https://thehackernews.com/2026/07/16-year-old-linux-kvm-flaw-lets-guest.html • https://www.openwall.com/lists/oss-security/2026/07/06/7 • https://securityonline.info/januscape-kvm-escape-cve-2026-53359-poc/
ATT&CKT1068 T1611
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Lightweight VMMs not on the allowlist (e.g. cloud-hypervisor forks, gVisor/runsc, Weston/Android emulators) legitimately opening /dev/kvm
  • Capability probes: kvm-ok, virt-host-validate, systemd-detect-virt run by config-management (Ansible/Puppet)
  • CI runners that spin nested KVM for kernel/image builds
  • Container runtimes with KVM passthrough (Kata, Firecracker under containerd) invoked by a non-listed wrapper
  • GPU/PCI-passthrough tooling that touches /dev/kvm during device setup
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("ansible","python3","runsc","containerd","containerd-shim") or ProcessCommandLine has_any ("open","O_RDWR")
Response runbook
1) Triage: identify the process image, parent, and account — is it a known VMM/admin tool, and is the account unprivileged? Confirm whether the host runs multi-tenant guests and whether /dev/kvm is world-writable (stat /dev/kvm). 2) Contain: if the opener is unexpected and non-service, isolate the host from the guest fleet, tighten /dev/kvm to root/kvm group (chmod 660, kvm group), and snapshot the process/binary for analysis. 3) Hunt: pivot on the same account/binary for prior compilations, downloads of Januscape/kvmCTF PoC artifacts, and correlate with UC-2 (host kernel panic) and UC-3 (unpatched kernel missing commit 81ccda30b4e8).
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(14d)
| where ProcessCommandLine has "/dev/kvm"
| where FileName !in~ ("qemu-system-x86_64","qemu-system-i386","qemu-kvm","qemu","libvirtd","virtqemud","cloud-hypervisor","firecracker","crosvm","kata-runtime","virt-host-validate","kvm-ok")
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("libvirtd","virtqemud","systemd")
| where AccountName !in~ ("root","libvirt-qemu","qemu")   // world-writable /dev/kvm path is exploited by UNPRIVILEGED users
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, FolderPath, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine
| order by Timestamp desc
Syslog
| where TimeGenerated > ago(14d)
| where SyslogMessage has "/dev/kvm"
| where SyslogMessage has_any ("type=SYSCALL","type=PATH","type=EXECVE","exe=")   // auditd records touching the device node
| where not(SyslogMessage has_any ("qemu","libvirt","cloud-hypervisor","firecracker","crosvm","kata","virt-host-validate","kvm-ok"))
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Facility, ProcessName, SyslogMessage
| order by TimeGenerated desc

KVM/x86 hosts unpatched for Januscape CVE-2026-53359 and chained Dirty Frag CVEs AIExploitation High
Surfaces Linux hosts still exposed to CVE-2026-53359 and the Dirty Frag chain (CVE-2026-43284 xfrm-ESP, CVE-2026-43500 RxRPC) that the researcher noted can be combined for full compromise without guest root. This is the posture pivot that scopes which multi-tenant KVM hosts still need patch commit 81ccda30b4e8, prioritizing the response for UC-1 and UC-2. Rationale: Uses the three concrete CVE IDs from the article (Januscape plus the explicitly-named Dirty Frag chain the author says can be combined for full compromise) against vuln-management telemetry; deterministic CVE match makes this a clean prioritization list rather than a behavioral guess. Cross-checked against: • https://thehackernews.com/2026/07/16-year-old-linux-kvm-flaw-lets-guest.html • https://www.openwall.com/lists/oss-security/2026/07/06/7
ATT&CKT1611 T1068
Data sourcesVulnerabilities.Vulnerabilities
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Hosts flagged by scanner metadata lag after patch (commit 81ccda30b4e8) is applied but package version string unchanged
  • Non-hypervisor Linux hosts (no KVM guests) reported vulnerable to the kernel CVE but not actually exposing the guest-to-host surface
  • Backported vendor kernels where the scanner mis-maps the fixed version
  • Containers/appliances inheriting the host kernel double-counted per instance
  • Air-gapped or decommissioned hosts still in the asset inventory
Response runbook
1) Triage: rank returned hosts by whether they run untrusted/multi-tenant guests and by internet exposure; verify true state with `git log --oneline | grep 81ccda30b4e8`-equivalent kernel version check. 2) Contain: for confirmed-vulnerable multi-tenant hosts, schedule emergency kernel patching/live-patch and, as interim mitigation, restrict /dev/kvm permissions and limit guest provisioning. 3) Hunt: on any host still unpatched, correlate against UC-1 (/dev/kvm access) and UC-2 (kernel panic) to determine whether exposure has already been exercised.

2026-07-07 6 use cases 4 techniques 6 kill-chain phases detected

Software supply chain security was hard enough. Then AI joined the build pipeline. For five years, "software supply chain security" meant one question: what's in your code? Which open-source packages, which versions, which transitive dependencies three layers deep that nobody chose on purpose? SolarWinds, Log4Shell, and XZ Utils all taught the same lesson: the risk lives less in the code a

Reconnaissance. Attacker researches the target — OSINT, scanning, enumeration.
Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad).
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code. → Trusted vendor binary / installer launching unusual children
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key. → Suspicious browser extension installation
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking.
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage. → Infostealer — non-browser process accessing browser cookie/login DBs · Ransomware-style mass file rename / extension change · LSASS process access / dump (credential theft) · Remote service execution — PsExec / SMB lateral movement
Suspicious browser extension installation Installation Medium
Side-loaded / unsigned extensions, often masquerading as wallets, productivity tools.
ATT&CKT1176
Data sourcesEndpoint.Registry DeviceRegistryEvents
DeviceRegistryEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)

| where RegistryKey has_any ("\Software\Google\Chrome\Extensions\","\Software\Microsoft\Edge\Extensions\","\Software\Mozilla\Firefox\Extensions\")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, RegistryKey, RegistryValueName, RegistryValueData,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessAccountName

| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)

| where RegistryKey has_any (@"\Software\Google\Chrome\Extensions\",
                              @"\Software\Microsoft\Edge\Extensions\",
                              @"\Software\Mozilla\Firefox\Extensions\")
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, RegistryKey,
          RegistryValue, RegistryValueData, ActingProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc

title: Infostealer - Non-Browser Process Accessing Browser Credential Stores
id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d01
status: experimental
description: |
    Stealers (RedLine, Lumma, Vidar, Atomic) read Login Data / cookies
    SQLite databases from Chrome/Edge/Firefox profile directories. Any
    non-browser process touching these files is a high-fidelity signal.
references:
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1539/
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1555/003/
author: Clankerusecase
date: 2026/05/02
tags:
    - attack.t1539
    - attack.t1555.003
    - attack.credential-access
logsource:
    category: file_access
    product: windows
detection:
    selection_path:
        TargetFilename|contains:
            - '\Google\Chrome\User Data\'
            - '\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\'
            - '\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\'
    selection_file:
        TargetFilename|endswith:
            - '\Login Data'
            - '\Cookies'
            - '\logins.json'
            - '\cookies.sqlite'
    filter_browser:
        Image|endswith:
            - '\chrome.exe'
            - '\msedge.exe'
            - '\firefox.exe'
            - '\brave.exe'
            - '\opera.exe'
    condition: selection_path and selection_file and not filter_browser
falsepositives:
    - Backup utilities reading user profile files
    - Browser sync agents from non-stock vendors
level: high
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem
    where (Filesystem.file_path="*\Google\Chrome\User Data\*\Login Data*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Google\Chrome\User Data\*\Cookies*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\*\Login Data*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\*\logins.json*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\*\cookies.sqlite*")
      AND NOT Filesystem.process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe","brave.exe","opera.exe")
    by Filesystem.dest, Filesystem.process_name, Filesystem.file_path, Filesystem.user
| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem
    where (Filesystem.file_path="*\Google\Chrome\User Data\*\Login Data*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Google\Chrome\User Data\*\Cookies*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\*\Login Data*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\*\logins.json*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\*\cookies.sqlite*")
      AND NOT Filesystem.process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe","brave.exe","opera.exe")
    by Filesystem.dest, Filesystem.process_name, Filesystem.file_path, Filesystem.user
| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`
Ransomware-style mass file rename / extension change Actions on Objectives Medium
Threshold detection: many files renamed in short window, often with new extension.
ATT&CKT1486
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem DeviceFileEvents
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
| where ActionType in ("FileRenamed","FileModified")
| summarize files = dcount(FileName) by DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, bin(Timestamp, 1m)
| where files > 200    // empirical: > 200 unique-file renames in 1m by one account on one host
                       //            is well above the P99 of legitimate bulk-tooling
| order by files desc

ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)
| where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
| where EventType in ("FileRenamed","FileModified")
| summarize files = dcount(TargetFileName)
            by DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName, bin(TimeGenerated, 1m)
| where files > 200    // P99 of legit bulk-tooling per-minute rename volume
| order by files desc
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count, dc(Filesystem.file_name) AS files
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem
    where Filesystem.action IN ("modified","renamed")
    by Filesystem.dest, Filesystem.user, _time span=1m
| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`
| where files > 200
| sort - files
| tstats summariesonly=false count, dc(Filesystem.file_name) AS files
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem
    where Filesystem.action IN ("modified","renamed")
    by Filesystem.dest, Filesystem.user, _time span=1m
| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`
| where files > 200
| sort - files
LSASS process access / dump (credential theft) Actions on Objectives High
Mimikatz, comsvcs.dll MiniDump, or any non-Windows process opening LSASS.
ATT&CKT1003.001 T1003
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes DeviceEvents
DeviceEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| where ActionType == "OpenProcessApiCall"
| where FileName =~ "lsass.exe"
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("MsSense.exe","MsMpEng.exe","csrss.exe",
                                          "svchost.exe","wininit.exe","services.exe",
                                          "lsm.exe","SearchProtocolHost.exe")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessFolderPath, AccountName
| order by Timestamp desc
// SecurityEvent EventID 4663 = object access. AccessMask 0x10 / 0x40 / 0x1010
// indicate read access to lsass.exe — credential-dump signature. Audit
// Object Access > Audit File System policy required.
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventID == 4663
| where ObjectName endswith "\lsass.exe"
| where Account !endswith "$"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, ObjectName, ProcessName,
          AccessMask, AccessReason
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Remote service execution — PsExec / SMB lateral movement Actions on Objectives High
psexec / paexec / smbexec / wmic /node — service install over SMB from remote host.
ATT&CKT1021.002 T1569.002
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes DeviceProcessEvents
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| where FileName in~ ("psexec.exe","psexesvc.exe","paexec.exe","smbexec.py")

| order by TimeGenerated desc
